docs.title: The vendored resistance algorithm
docs.text:
crates/ligase-core/rulesets/ holds Stanford's HIVdb algorithm definitions, unmodified and pinned by SHA-256. They come from hivdb/hivfacts, which carries the Unlicense — a dedication to the public domain — so redistributing them here is unencumbered.

Neither hivdb/sierra (GPL-3.0) nor hivdb/asi_interpreter (Apache-2.0) contributed any code to Ligase. The licence, the provenance of each file and the citation Stanford asks for are recorded in rulesets/README.md.

docs.title: Intended use
docs.text: Ligase is research software. Its drug-resistance calls are not for clinical use — see the README.

docs.title: Milestones and Acceptance Tests
docs.text: One milestone per session. Plan → write tests → implement → write docs.

docs.title: M0 — Scaffold
docs.text:
Cargo workspace (ligase-core, ligase-py), maturin, python/ligase, CI running fmt, clippy, ruff, mypy, cargo test, pytest.

Done when: pip install -e . works and import ligase succeeds in CI.

docs.title: M1 — Types and dimensions
docs.text: Done when: - HXB2 FASTA and a sample BAM are loaded with dimensions inferred from headers. - A BAM aligned to a different reference fails check() with a clear DimensionError. - A chr1 vs 1 mismatch raises a distinct error.

docs.title: M2 — Graph
docs.text: Done when: the golden example builds a graph without executing anything, and ligase check reports all type errors in one pass.

docs.title: M3 — Execution and cache
docs.text: Done when: - The demo runs end to end on 3–4 runs from PRJNA517147. - A second run completes entirely from cache. - Changing min_freq reruns only call and resistance. - Adding one sample processes only that sample.

docs.title: M4 — Semantic hashing and early cutoff
docs.text: Done when: rerunning alignment with a different thread count produces the same canonical hash and downstream steps are skipped.

docs.title: M5 — Provenance
docs.text: Done when: ligase methods outputs a methods paragraph with tool versions, parameters, reference accession and citations, plus a bundle that reproduces the results on a clean machine.

docs.title: M6 — Validation
docs.text:
Done when: resistance calls match published results for PRJNA517147 and the Sanger ground truth for PRJNA1218827, with discrepancies explained.

Done. The calls are checked against the published Stanford HIVdb reports for PRJNA1218827: 81 of 81 drug calls agree exactly at the 15% and 5% thresholds, and the three that differ at 2% each carry a cause. The scoring engine separately reproduces 3,348 published expectations.

There were nine. Six of them were an artefact of reading codons from a VCF, which carries no phasing, and went when codons started being read from the haplotypes the reads carry (D31).

PRJNA517147 could not serve as a source of expected answers: its per-sample calls are published only as colour in a heatmap, reverse transcriptase only. It remains the demo'''s default dataset. See validation.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
How .ligase/ is laid out, how a key is composed, and what each choice costs. The user-facing account is Running, and not running.

Everything here lives in crates/ligase-core/src/: hash.rs, key.rs and cache.rs. None of it knows about Python.

docs.title: The directory
docs.text:
.ligase/
├── cache.sqlite          metadata: keys, outputs, file hashes
├── store/                content-addressed objects
│   └── 3c/73431de6...eeaa85.tsv
└── tmp/                  staging, for steps that are still running

Three properties are deliberate.

The store is fanned out over the first byte of the hash. A cohort of four hundred samples through five steps is two thousand objects; a flat directory of those is a directory no filesystem enjoys. One level of 256 buckets is enough for the sizes this tool is for.

An object keeps its suffix. samtools sort -o x.bam writes BAM and x.sam writes SAM: tools read the format off the name, so an object called 3c73… with no extension is an object no tool will read correctly. Everything after the first dot survives, which is what keeps .vcf.gz intact.

Staging is inside the cache directory. Moving a finished output into the store is then a rename rather than a copy — a 24 GB BAM copied once more per run would be a real cost — and a crashed run leaves its debris somewhere a user can delete wholesale.

Stored objects are made read-only. The store is the cache's evidence: a step that wrote back through one of its inputs would invalidate every key derived from it without anything noticing.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE meta  (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE files (path TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    size INTEGER NOT NULL,
                    mtime_ns INTEGER NOT NULL,
                    hash TEXT NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE steps (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    step TEXT NOT NULL,
                    output_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
                    suffix TEXT NOT NULL,
                    tools TEXT NOT NULL,
                    duration_ms INTEGER NOT NULL,
                    created_at TEXT NOT NULL);

SQLite because D6 says so: zero-config, embedded, portable, and — the part that matters for a reproducibility tool — openable with sqlite3 when a result needs explaining. A faster key-value store that can only be read by the program that wrote it would be a worse trade here.

rusqlite is used with the bundled feature, which compiles SQLite from source. That costs a C compiler at build time, which is a real concession given that D11 chose pure-Rust format parsing precisely to avoid one. It buys one identical SQLite everywhere, which an on-disk format that outlives a single run needs more than it needs a shorter build.

duration_ms and tools are not used for cache decisions. They are there because the next question after "was this cached?" is "how long did it take when it did run, and with what?" — and because M5 will want them.

docs.title: Versioning, and why nothing is migrated
docs.text:
Two version numbers sit in meta.

schema_version describes the directory layout. A directory written by another version has its tables dropped.

key_version describes how keys are composed (key::KEY_VERSION). A mismatch deletes every row of steps, and keeps files.

That asymmetry is the whole point. A file's hash is a fact about the file, true regardless of how keys are made. A step's entry is a claim that these ingredients, combined this way produced that output — so a key from another format is not stale data to be migrated, it is a claim about something else. Reading it would be the one failure mode a cache must never have.

Nothing is migrated because nothing needs to be: every byte in here is derived, and the cost of being wrong is enormously higher than the cost of recomputing.

docs.title: The prefilter
docs.text:
Cache::content_hash consults files by (path, size, mtime_ns). A hit returns the stored hash without opening the file; a miss hashes it and records the result.

Three details keep this honest.

A timestamp can only ever save work. It never contributes to a hash and never to a key. The direction of the bet matters: a stale timestamp causes a rehash (a cost), never a wrong answer — except in the one case below.

The file is re-stat'd after hashing. A file written while we were hashing it would otherwise be remembered under the size and mtime it had before, and every later run would trust that hash. If the stat moved, the hash is used for this run and not recorded.

The miss case is a file edited in place, keeping its exact length, within one timestamp granularity. This is the residual risk of D3, it is documented rather than hidden, and --force is the answer. The alternative — hashing every input on every run — makes looking at a 40 GB BAM cost minutes, which turns content addressing from a feature into something users route around.

Cache::stats() counts hits and misses, which is where report.hashed and report.prefiltered come from. It exists so the prefilter is testable: asserting that a second run read nothing is how you find out it is working, and no amount of staring at output tells you that.

docs.title: The key
docs.text:
pub struct Ingredients {
    pub step: String,                      // the step's name
    pub code: String,                      // its source, as written
    pub recipe: String,                    // the command, or "callback"
    pub output: DataKind,                  // what it declares it produces
    pub parameters: Vec<(String, String)>, // (name, value)
    pub inputs: Vec<(String, ContentHash)>,// (parameter, content hash)
    pub tools: Vec<(String, String)>,      // (name, version)
}

Hashed with BLAKE3, every field length-prefixed. The length prefixes are not decoration: concatenating would make a parameter x with value yz indistinguishable from a parameter xy with value z, and a cache key that can confuse two different inputs is a wrong answer waiting for the right coincidence. There is a test for exactly that pair.

Names bind, order does not. Inputs, parameters and tools are sorted by name before hashing, so the order they were collected in cannot change a key — but which name a value is bound to very much does, because the same two files swapped between aln and ref is a different command.

The composition is pinned by a test that asserts a literal key for a fixed set of ingredients. That makes an accidental change to the layout a failing test rather than a silently cold cache for every user of the release; it is meant to be updated deliberately, together with KEY_VERSION.

code is the function's source as written, read with inspect.getsource. The consequence is worth stating plainly: a comment-only edit reruns the step. That is the safe direction — too cold costs time, too warm produces a wrong answer — and early cutoff stops the rerun going any further. For a function with no source to read (a REPL, an exec), the compiled code object stands in.

docs.title: What an input's hash is a hash of
docs.text:
Inputs enter as content hashes tagged with the policy that produced them. Since M4 that is INPUT_POLICY = "canonical": the hash of what a file means rather than of its bytes (D4) — sorted records, volatile headers such as @PG lines and timestamps stripped, as canonicalisation defines per type.

It arrived exactly as this page said it would, which is worth recording because it was the point of putting the tag in before needing it: the policy name changed, KEY_VERSION went to 2, the old entries retired themselves, and nothing in the shape of Ingredients moved. Runner::key asks Cache::semantic_hash(kind, path) where it asked Cache::content_hash.

Three things sit in meta now rather than two, and they are cleared differently. A layout change drops the tables; a key-format change deletes the step entries; a change to the canonicalisation rules (CANON_VERSION) deletes the canonical hashes and the step entries built from them. The files table survives all three, because a file's byte hash is a fact about the file however keys are made.

The store still names objects after their bytes, deliberately: an object's name is a claim about its contents that anyone can check with b3sum. The canonical hash is a derived fact held beside it, in the canonical table, keyed on the byte hash rather than on a path — so a file moved, copied, or produced identically by another step is parsed once in its life.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text: Provenance. This layer records that a key produced an output, with the tool versions and the duration, because it had them. It does not record why a result is what it is — the command, the references, the citations, the methods paragraph. That lives in provenance.sqlite, beside this database and deliberately not in it: "has this been computed?" and "what would I write in a paper?" want different lifetimes, and this one's tables are dropped whenever a key format moves (D23). See provenance.

docs.title: Canonicalisation
docs.text:
crates/ligase-core/src/canon/ — one module per format, plus the digest they all build. No pyo3: deciding whether two files mean the same thing is correctness-critical logic, and it is tested in Rust.

The job: (DataKind, path) → ContentHash, over a byte stream that depends on what the file says and not on how it was written.

docs.title: Why this exists at all
docs.text:
M3 keyed a step on its inputs' bytes, and documented early cutoff as following from it: a step that reruns and writes the same bytes leaves every key below it alone. That is true, and on real tools it almost never happened.

minimap2 writes its whole command line into @PG CL. The command line includes the output path. The output path is .ligase/tmp/<key>.bam. So a step's output bytes contain that step's own key, and any change to the step — a parameter, a tool version, a comment — moved its bytes, which moved the key of the step below, whose bytes then moved in turn. The cascade ran to the bottom of the pipeline.

bcftools has the same shape with a timestamp added: ##bcftools_callCommand=call -mv ... -o /tmp/out.vcf.gz; Date=Sat Oct 17 21:14:12 2026.

M4 is therefore less "widen a strict test" than "make the cutoff M3 described actually hold". The thread-count acceptance criterion in docs/milestones.md is one instance of it.

docs.title: Where it attaches
docs.text:
Exactly where the cache said it would.

pub const INPUT_POLICY: &str = "canonical";   // was "raw"
pub const KEY_VERSION: u32 = 2;               // was 1

Ingredients did not change shape. Runner::key now asks Cache::semantic_hash(kind, path) where it asked Cache::content_hash, and the kind comes from the graph — the input node's dataset — rather than from the step.

The store still names objects after their bytes. That is deliberate: an object's name is a claim about its contents that anyone can check with b3sum. The canonical hash is a derived fact held beside it, not a replacement for it.

docs.title: The digest
docs.text:
canon::Digest is the only thing that writes bytes into the hash, and it offers two ways to do it.

  • field(label, value) — written immediately, in order. For anything whose position means something.
  • record(parts) — hashed to 32 bytes now, collected, and sorted at the end. For anything whose position does not.

Everything is length-prefixed, so a field x = yz cannot produce the same stream as xy = z. The domain, the rules' version, the DataKind and whether this is a canonical form or a fallback all go in first, so no two of those can collide.

Records are sorted as digests, not as text: 32 bytes a record rather than a few hundred, which matters on a BAM with a hundred million of them. A sorted list of digests is still a commitment to the whole multiset — duplicates and absences included, which a commutative combination such as an XOR would lose.

docs.title: Which formats sort
docs.text:
Kind In order Sorted Dropped Reads — records the description after a name; the + line's repeat Reference contigs — descriptions, line wrapping, case Alignment @SQ records @HD, @PG, @CO; @RG is sorted by ID Variants ##contig, samples records see below Intervals — records track, browser, # ResistanceReport the header row the rows below it trailing blanks

The split is not a new judgement. It is D14, which already decided that a sequence dictionary's order is semantic (GATK insists on it) while a BED's record order is incidental. A reference is a sequence dictionary, so it keeps its order; @SQ is one, so it keeps its order; records are not, so they sort.

docs.title: Alignment
docs.text:
Parsed by noodles, BAM and SAM through one code path over the sam::alignment::Record trait. That is what makes a BAM hash the same as the SAM it came from, which D9 requires: re-encoding is not a biological change, so samtools view -b must not cost a cache.

Each record contributes name, flags, reference id, position, mapping quality, CIGAR, mate reference and position, template length, sequence, qualities, and its tags.

Tags are kept, all of them, sorted by tag. They are results — NM, AS, ms are what the aligner concluded — and keeping an unknown tag is the conservative direction. What is normalised away is incidental: the order they were written in, and an integer's storage width, so a SAM's NM:i:3 and a BAM's single byte are the same 3.

@RG keeps ID and SM and nothing else. The rest of a read group is metadata, and one of its standard tags is DT — a date.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
noodles reads and validates the header. The records are then canonicalised as text: tab-split, validated (eight columns or more, a numeric POS), with QUAL quantised and the INFO and FILTER keys sorted.

The alternative was to rebuild each record from the typed accessors, and it was rejected. Doing so means choosing a rendering for every INFO value type, and a rendering that differs from the tool's own is a fresh chance to call two identical results different. What is being compared here is two outputs of the same tool, and for that the tool's own text is the most faithful record of what it concluded. What is normalised is only what is genuinely incidental — DP=10;AF=0.5 and AF=0.5;DP=10 are one set of annotations written two ways.

ALT is deliberately left in its order: a genotype's 1 means the first alternate allele, so sorting them would renumber every call in the file. FORMAT and the sample columns are left alone for the same reason — they line up with each other positionally.

Header keys dropped: fileDate, fileDay, source, reference, bcftoolsVersion, and any key ending Command, CommandLine, Version or Date — which covers bcftools_callCommand, bcftools_viewVersion, GATKCommandLine and whatever the next tool calls its own.

##reference is worth stating separately: it holds a path, and docs/dimensions.md is explicit that reference identity never rests on a filename. load::variants already refuses to read identity from it. The ##contig lines carry it, and they are kept.

INFO and FORMAT definitions keep their ID, Number and Type and drop their Description: which fields a record can carry, and how they are shaped, is part of what the file is; the prose describing them is not, and a tool release that rewords a description has not changed a call. Number is spelled out by hand (A, R, G, ., LA…) rather than taken from a derived Debug, so that a rename inside noodles cannot quietly change what every key in every cache is made of.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Scanned by hand, as load::fasta is, so that a three-gigabase reference is reduced without being held in memory: each contig's sequence is folded into a hash of its own as it is read. The line breaks arrive as nothing but the points between updates, which is why wrapping cannot reach the result.

Uppercased, because that is the form the SAM specification defines its M5 contig checksum over, and ReferenceId::fingerprint already agrees. Soft masking goes with the case, deliberately: a lowercased repeat region is an annotation applied to a sequence, not a different sequence.

docs.title: Reads, intervals, report
docs.text: FASTQ through noodles, which has already split the description off the name. BED by hand, as load::intervals is, because noodles' BED reader is typed by column count and a BED in the wild has whichever columns its author felt like writing. The resistance report is ours: the header row kept as a row, the rows below it sorted, and a row whose column count disagrees with the header is a parse failure rather than something to hash.

docs.title: Tolerance
docs.text:
pub struct Tolerance(f64);
impl Tolerance { pub fn bucket(self, value: f64) -> Option<i64>; }
pub fn tolerance(kind: DataKind, field: &str) -> Option<Tolerance>;

One table, one entry: (Variants, "QUAL") at 0.1. Everything else is exact.

A tolerance can only be expressed by quantising, and D20 says why: "within ε" is not transitive, so it is not an equality, and a hash can only express an equality.

0.1 Phred is chosen to absorb last-digit floating-point wobble — 215.376 against 215.375 — while sitting two orders of magnitude below the smallest threshold anyone filters on, so it cannot merge two qualities a user would treat differently. It is one constant in one table.

A value too large to bucket keeps its own text rather than being folded in with every other large value, and a QUAL of . is kept as written: there is nothing to quantise and nothing is gained by pretending otherwise.

docs.title: The fallback
docs.text:
A file that will not parse hashes as its bytes, tagged Form::Raw (D21). The tag is inside the digest, so a fallback can never collide with a canonical form, nor with the plain ContentHash of the same bytes.

The direction matters: bytes are the stricter test, so a fallback can cost a rerun and can never serve a wrong answer. It is also what keeps the engine working on a .bam holding something that is not a BAM — including the text-file fixtures the execution tests are built on.

Every parser is strict for the same reason. A canonicaliser that read what it could and ignored the rest would be the dangerous kind of lenient: two files that differ only in the part it skipped would agree, which is the one failure a cache must never have. So a FASTA with no > line, a BED row with two columns, a VCF record with seven, and a report row that does not fit its header are all parse failures.

docs.title: What a canonical form notices
docs.text:
The fallback handles a file that will not parse. The other half of the same problem is a file that parses perfectly and is still wrong in a field the rules cannot drop, and that is what a Note is for (D26).

There is one note in v0.1: a sample identifier that is a file. A VCF's sample names and a BAM's read-group samples are what the file is about — a sample set is a dimension — so neither can go the way @PG went, and a tool handed an alignment with no @RG SM writes the input file's path there. The hash of such an output moves with the cache root.

Note::about_sample decides, and deliberately narrowly: a path separator, or a trailing extension naming a format this engine reads. K03455.1 has a dot and is not a file. The Shape it finds — absolute, relative or a bare name — only chooses the wording, because an absolute path is the one that cannot travel and saying so is more use than "a file".

for sample in header.sample_names() {
    digest.text("sample", sample);
    if let Some(note) = Note::about_sample(sample) {
        digest.note(note);
    }
}

Three properties hold, and each is a test:

  • A note never changes a hash. Digest::note pushes onto a Vec that finish does not read. Two VCFs differing only in a path-shaped sample still have different hashes, because they are claims about different sample sets.
  • A note is dropped on the fallback path. canon::hash takes the notes out of the digest on success and discards them on failure. A remark about a file that did not parse would be a remark about the half of it that was read.
  • Repeats collapse. Digest::note ignores a note it already holds, so an alignment whose four read groups name the same file has one thing wrong with it rather than four.

docs.title: Where a note goes
docs.text:
Canonical carries notes beside hash and form, and from there they travel without being recomputed:

Layer What it does with them Cache::semantic Stores them in the canonical table beside the hash, and hands them back on a cache hit. semantic_hash keeps its old signature for callers that only want the hash. exec::StepResult A notes field on every finished step, printed by exec::render as a noticed line with the advice stated once per kind (D15). prov::Record output_notes, in a produced_notes child table. This is why PROV_VERSION is 2. prov::Methods A Noticed per node — not per group, since a group is nodes run the same way and four samples run identically can be named after four different files. Methods::notices() gathers them by step and kind. bundle A notes.tsv table, a What was noticed section in the README, and, for the notes that can explain a hash that moved, Verification::noticed from the run being checked.

They are stored rather than recomputed because a cache hit does not reopen the file, and a warning that appeared on the first run and vanished on the second would be worse than no warning. That is the one cost: the cache's SCHEMA_VERSION moved to 2 for the new column, which clears its tables. CANON_VERSION did not move, because nothing about what is hashed changed.

Canonicalisation is not the only thing that finds a note. A step's body says what its own work rested on, which no reading of the output could recover, and those notes travel the same way — stored against the step's key rather than the output's hash, since they are not facts about its bytes. The Note type itself, both producers and every surface a note reaches are in Notes.

docs.title: What it costs, and why it is paid once
docs.text:
Canonicalising a BAM is a full pass over it. Doing that on every run would be the one thing that makes this unaffordable, so it is remembered:

CREATE TABLE canonical (
    raw       TEXT NOT NULL,   -- the hash of the file's bytes
    kind      TEXT NOT NULL,
    canonical TEXT NOT NULL,
    form      TEXT NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (raw, kind)
)

Keyed on the hash of the bytes, not on the path, because that is what it is a fact about. A file moved, copied, or produced again identically by another step is not parsed twice. Behind it sits the prefilter, so the steady state of a second run is stat → remembered byte hash → remembered canonical hash, and report.hashed and report.canonicalised are both zero.

CANON_VERSION sits in the cache's meta beside the other two versions. A change to it clears this table and the step entries, which is D19 extended by one line: a canonical hash is a fact about a file given the rules that produced it, so one computed under other rules is a fact about something else. Nothing is migrated because nothing needs to be.

docs.title: Audit mode
docs.text:
crates/ligase-core/src/audit.rs, which is the user-facing half of the same idea: comparing bytes and meaning separately is what lets an audit tell a tool that signs its work from a tool that cannot repeat itself.

pub enum Verdict { Deterministic, Reproducible, NotReproducible }

audit() runs the pipeline once, normally and through the cache, so that the audited nodes have their inputs; then runs each of them twice more through exec::produce into scratch files, hashes each output both ways, and deletes the scratch. Nothing from the two runs is recorded: an audit observes, and recording either would put a result from a step known to wobble into the cache.

Two pieces were lifted out of exec rather than duplicated — exec::inputs_of, so an audited step is handed exactly what a run would hand it, and exec::produce, which is the part of running a step that is just running it. The audited nodes are taken in turn: a duration is part of what an audit reports, and two runs of an aligner competing for cores would produce timings that describe the machine rather than the step.

AuditReport::verdict() is the worst verdict, not the commonest. One irreproducible sample in a cohort is an irreproducible step, and a summary that averaged them would bury what the user is auditing for — the same reasoning as D15 counting places rather than names.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text:
Provenance. Nothing here records why a result is what it is — and dropping the fields that used to say so is what made provenance necessary rather than merely nice (D22).

Notes about inputs. A note is reported for what a run produced. A leaf input the user supplied with path-shaped sample names is their file, described as they gave it, and exec::remember records an InputRecord without notes. Reporting those would mean deciding what a user is to do about a file the pipeline did not write.

BCF and CRAM. Both would fall back to their bytes today. Neither is in the reference pipeline; adding them is a module beside the others and a CANON_VERSION bump.

Sorting under memory pressure. Record digests are held in memory while a file is canonicalised: 32 bytes a record, so a hundred million records is 3.2 GB. That is fine for the amplicon data this is built on and would need an external sort for whole-genome BAMs. The shape that would change is Digest::finish, and nothing above it.

Deciding whether two different tools agree. Everything here is built to compare two outputs of the same tool. A canonical form that could reconcile a GATK VCF with a bcftools one is a much larger claim, and the right place for it is the conversion graph (D5), not the hash.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
How a checked graph becomes parallel work. The cache it consults is described separately; this is about who runs what, where, and why Python is not in the loop.

Lives in crates/ligase-core/src/exec.rs, with the Python side in python/ligase/graph.py (Pipeline.run, Pipeline._plan) and the binding in crates/ligase-py/src/lib.rs.

docs.title: Recipes are extracted before anything runs
docs.text:
A step's body is Python. A run is a few dozen external processes over tens of gigabytes. Those two facts pull in opposite directions: if the scheduler had to call into Python to find out what each step does, the GIL would sit in the hot path of every parallel run.

So it does not. The body is called once, before the run starts, and what it returns is a recipe:

return lg.sh("minimap2 -ax sr {ref} {reads.r1} {reads.r2} | samtools sort -o {out}")

That is a Shell holding a template — a pure value, no paths in it, nothing read. Pipeline._plan collects one per step node, together with the function's source, its plain parameters and its tools, and hands the core a complete description of the work. The core then owns the whole run with the GIL released, and a cohort of shell steps runs at full width.

This is only possible because bodies were already deferred (D12): a body that computed something could not be called before its inputs existed. A body that describes work can.

The one exception is lg.write, whose work genuinely is Python. The core schedules it like any other step and takes the GIL to call it, through a Host trait so that nothing in the core knows Python exists:

pub trait Host: Sync {
    fn call(&self, id: u64, out: &Path, inputs: &[(String, Vec<PathBuf>)])
        -> Result<(), String>;
}

Those steps serialise against each other. For an interpretation step that is the right trade; for anything doing real work it is the wrong one, which the guide says out loud.

docs.title: The scheduler
docs.text:
Index order is dependency order — a node can only name earlier ones (the graph) — so there is no topological sort to do. What is left is a ready queue:

  • remaining[node] counts unfinished upstream steps (input nodes are already there).
  • A node whose count reaches zero joins ready.
  • A step runs, then decrements its dependents and starts whichever of them that emptied.

The state sits behind one Mutex, and each step is one rayon job on a pool sized to --jobs. A job that finishes starts the steps it released before it ends, so the run is over exactly when the scope is empty: it cannot empty while anything can still start.

Rayon rather than Python threads is the direct consequence of recipes being extracted up front: there is no interpreter to re-enter, so the pool is just a pool. It is also already in the tree for BLAKE3's multi-threaded hashing of large files.

docs.title: Nothing waits for work
docs.text:
No worker loops looking for the next step and none blocks waiting for one. That is not a style preference; it is what keeps the pool safe to reuse from inside a step.

A step hashes its own inputs, and BLAKE3 hashes a large file across whatever pool it is called from (D3) — so a step queues work on the executor's own pool as a matter of course. Rayon can only give that work to a worker it believes is idle. The first version of this scheduler held every spare worker blocked on a Condvar of its own, inside a scope.spawn job, which rayon counts as busy: hashing inside a step was left with no one able to help it, and under heavy load a run stopped for good (D27).

A worker can still block where rayon cannot see it — on a step's own child process, or on the GIL inside a callback. The invariant is narrower than "a worker never blocks": a worker must never block on something that needs the pool to make progress. A child process and the GIL do not; the ready queue and a claimed key did.

Two tests in tests/execution.rs pin this. Each has a step queue work on the pool it is running on and wait for it with a timeout, once while another step is waiting its turn and once while a twin key is waiting — the two places a worker used to block. They fail in about ten seconds against the old scheduler rather than hanging, so a regression is a red test and not a cargo test that never returns.

docs.title: One key, one piece of work
docs.text:
Two nodes can share a key — the same step over identical data, which happens more often in a cohort than you would expect. Running both would be the same work twice, and under a thread pool the second would not even see the first's cache entry.

So a key is claimed for the duration of a step. A node that wants a claimed key is parked on it — recorded under that key and abandoned, with its worker handed straight back to rayon. When the holder drops the claim it puts everything parked on its key back on the ready queue, and those nodes start again from the top: they recompute the key, find it in the cache this time, and report a hit.

Parking rather than waiting is the same rule as above. A worker blocked on a claimed key is a worker rayon counts as busy, and therefore one that cannot help the very step it is waiting for (D27). Parking also costs no --jobs slot: a waiting node used to occupy a worker doing nothing.

The alternative — letting both run and relying on the store to deduplicate identical bytes — is correct but wasteful, and makes "how many times did this run?" unanswerable. For a tool whose job is to not redo work, that is the wrong default.

docs.title: Filling in a command
docs.text:
{name}, {name.r1}, {name.r2} and {out} are resolved against the step's own parameters; {{ and }} are literal braces.

Two decisions here are about failure modes rather than features.

Unknown placeholders are an error. {refrence} is a typo, and a shell handed the literal text would either fail obscurely much later or — with echo — succeed. The cost is that an awk '{print $1}' has to be written '{{print $1}}', which is Snakemake's convention and so already familiar to the people this is for. Anything between braces that is not an identifier is reported as a brace needing escaping rather than as a mistyped placeholder, because that is the thing the user has to change.

Every substituted value is one shell word, single-quoted, with embedded quotes escaped. A reference under /my refs/ is one path, not two arguments, and a value cannot end the quoting and continue as code.

docs.title: Failure is per node, and independent branches continue
docs.text:
A step that fails is recorded against its node, with the tool's own stderr and the exit status. Then:

  • Independent branches keep running. Losing three good samples to one bad FASTQ is the overnight-run problem this project exists to remove.
  • Steps below a failure do not run, and are in neither list: one cause, one failure, rather than a cascade of "input missing" noise.
  • Nothing is recorded in the cache, so the staged output of a half-finished step can never be served as a result.

pipe.run() then raises RunError carrying the whole report, the same shape pipe.check() uses: every problem found before anything is raised, and the successes still reachable.

docs.title: Why the report is worded in Rust
docs.text:
exec::summarise and exec::render build the text, exactly as the check report is built in the core. Two surfaces print it — ligase run and report.text — and one wording for both is the only way they cannot drift.

Two rules carry over from D15, for the same reasons:

  • A step that ran gets its own line with its own cost, and the costs line up, because reading down a column is how you find the step that took the night.
  • Steps that did not run are grouped by outcome and their samples are named, not counted. A user who has to expand something to learn which four samples were cached has a shorter report, not a better one.

Results are sorted by node before rendering. Workers finish in whatever order the machine allows, and a reproducibility tool that printed two different reports for two identical runs would be an odd thing.

docs.title: What skipped means, and why it is not cached
docs.text:
Both are cache hits. The difference is whether anything above them ran.

Each finished node carries a flag: did this step, or anything above it, run in this run? A cache hit whose upstream flag is set is skipped — early cutoff — and one whose flag is clear is cached.

That distinction costs one boolean and answers the question a user actually has after an edit: did my change reach anything? "Everything cached" and "the step reran and changed nothing, so the rest was unnecessary" are very different pieces of news.

"Changed nothing" means the output's canonical form is unchanged, not its bytes (canonicalisation). With bytes, skipped was a verdict almost no real tool could earn: minimap2 records its command line in @PG, that command line holds the output path, and the output path is the staging file named after the step's own key — so a step's bytes moved whenever its key did. Every StepResult therefore carries both hashes, and the one below it is keyed on the second.

docs.title: What a run records besides its answer
docs.text:
A step that runs writes a provenance record naming the command that ran, with its placeholders filled in. It has to happen here: fill_template is the only thing that renders that command, and since M4 it is nowhere else — not in the cache, and not in the output, whose @PG line is dropped before hashing (D22). A step served from the cache writes nothing, because the record from the run that did the work is still there.

exec::produce therefore returns an Execution — the duration and the command — and exec::run takes a Stores { cache, prov }, so that "a run records provenance" shows up in the type rather than hiding in a constructor.

docs.title: What is deliberately absent
docs.text:
Turning those records into prose. A methods paragraph and a bundle are prov's business, built after a run rather than during one.

Running a step twice to find out whether it is reproducible is audit.rs, which borrows exec::produce and exec::inputs_of rather than repeating them (canonicalisation).

Cluster execution (D8). The scheduler assumes one machine and a shared filesystem. The ready-queue shape would survive a change of executor, but nothing has been built for one.

docs.title: Graph architecture
docs.text: How a pipeline is built from signatures, how dimensions travel through it, and why requirements come from the graph rather than from a table. The user-facing view is Pipelines and the graph.

docs.title: Where the code lives
docs.text:
crates/ligase-core/src/
  graph.rs          Graph, NodeId, Argument, StepSpec, propagation, check
  load/intervals.rs BED and GFF records
  check.rs          disagreements(), requires(), the errors the graph builds

crates/ligase-py/src/lib.rs   the Graph pyclass; translation only
python/ligase/graph.py        @lg.step, Step, StepOutput, Pipeline
python/ligase/samples.py      Samples and .map()
python/ligase/errors.py       the exception hierarchy
python/ligase/cli.py          `ligase check`

The graph is in ligase-core and has no pyo3 dependency, like everything else that must not be wrong. The Python layer reads signatures and calls add_step; it holds no checking logic, and all error wording is generated in Rust so the Rust tests own it.

docs.title: Deferral: how a body never runs
docs.text:
class Step(Generic[P, R]):
    def __call__(self, *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        bound = self._signature.bind(*args, **kwargs)
        bound.apply_defaults()
        return cast("R", StepOutput(self, dict(bound.arguments)))

inspect.signature and get_type_hints run once, at decoration. Calling the step binds the arguments — so a missing or surplus argument still fails at the call site, exactly as it would for the undecorated function — and returns a StepOutput.

That cast is a deliberate lie to the type checker, and it buys something real. A type checker sees align as (Reads, Reference) -> Alignment, so it follows the pipeline and catches a mis-wired one while you are editing:

pipe = lg.Pipeline(call(align(reads, hxb2), calls))  # error: Variants, not Reference

At runtime the value is a StepOutput, and lg.handle() is the typed way to reach it. The alternative — a handle class that really is a Dataset — would have meant putting graph identity on the data types, and a dataset that knows which graph it belongs to is a dataset that cannot be used in two.

check() catches the same mistake for code that is not type-checked, which is most pipelines in practice.

docs.title: Why annotations are mandatory
docs.text: An unannotated parameter is refused at decoration time, not at check time. A missing annotation on a dataset parameter would not be a missing label — it would be an edge the graph does not contain, so that input would never be compared with anything. Silently dropping a connection is the exact failure mode this project exists to remove, so the sooner it is said the better.

docs.title: Construction: cycles are unrepresentable
docs.text:
pub fn add_input(&mut self, label: &str, dataset: Dataset) -> NodeId
pub fn add_step(&mut self, spec: StepSpec) -> Result<NodeId, GraphError>

add_step takes NodeIds that already exist, so a node can only ever depend on an earlier one. There is no cycle detection in this module because there is nothing to detect: index order is dependency order, checking is a single forward pass, and no topological sort is needed anywhere.

Pipeline.__init__ walks back from the outputs, keyed by object identity, so a file passed to two steps becomes one node. Identity rather than equality is the right key: two datasets loaded from the same file are two nodes, because the user wrote them as two, and a cache that notices they are identical is the executor's job rather than the graph's.

docs.title: Propagation
docs.text:
A step's output carries the dimensions of its inputs, re-sourced as Source::Derived { step } — the variant M1 added and deliberately left unused.

for each dimension the output kind applies to:
    coordinates  -> introduced by the step (see below)
    otherwise    -> the first argument, in signature order, that states it
                    and, if none states it, that argument's own gap verbatim

Three details carry weight.

Signature order decides. Where two inputs both state a dimension, the first wins. They are also checked against each other, so a disagreement is already reported at this step; picking one keeps a single root cause from echoing down the rest of the pipeline as a second error.

An unknown keeps its reason. When nothing states a dimension, the output inherits the first applicable input's Unknown { reason } rather than a fresh one. "no @RG lines with an SM tag in the header" is still the instruction three steps later; "this step did not have one" would not be.

Coordinates are introduced, not inherited. Nothing upstream of an alignment has a coordinate system — FASTQ and FASTA have none — so inheriting would leave it unknown forever. Alignments and variant calls are 1-based closed by specification (D9). Intervals are the exception: a tool that writes BED from a VCF changes the convention, so a step producing Intervals must declare what it writes, and reports its coordinates as unknown until it does. Inheriting 1-based closed there would be a lie that passes check().

A pleasant side effect: a derived alignment knows its pairing from the reads it was built from, where M1 could only report an alignment's pairing as unknown because the information is in the SAM flags.

docs.title: Checking
docs.text:
pub fn check(&self, roots: &[NodeId]) -> Vec<CheckError>

One forward pass over the nodes the roots reach, in index order. Per step:

  1. Kinds. Each argument's supplied kind against the kind the step declared. A mismatch is reported instead of that step's dimension errors, not alongside them — the bindings are not what the step declared, so comparing their dimensions would describe a pipeline the user never wrote. One error per root cause.
  2. Disagreements. check::disagreements, which is M1's comparison logic with the requirements half removed.
  3. Requirements. Below.

roots restricts the walk, so a module that builds two pipelines checks each against its own outputs and an unreachable branch is nobody's problem.

docs.title: Requirements come from the graph
docs.text:
docs/dimensions.md:

Unknown dimensions are allowed only if no downstream step requires them.

M1 could not implement that sentence. Checking one step in isolation has no downstream, so check_step reads "required" off the pair of kinds in front of it (required_pair). That table is now the default, and the graph adds what the table cannot know: where the gap started.

for each dimension some step requires:
    for each argument that applies to it and does not know it:
        origin = walk the inheritance chain back to where it entered
        report once per (origin, dimension), naming the requiring step
                                            and the route between them

The walk follows exactly the rule propagation followed — the first argument that can speak to the dimension — so the origin is the node the value was supposed to come from. A step that introduces a dimension is its own origin, which is how a step that forgot to declare its coordinate system gets blamed rather than its input.

Two things follow, and both are about readability rather than about catching more.

The error names a file, not just a step. Without the graph the message points at merge, where the user can change nothing; with it the message points at the BAM, and says that it reaches merge through call.

One missing declaration is one error. Deduplicated on (origin, dimension), so a value that flows through five steps that all require it produces one error rather than five. A report nobody reads to the end is a report that does not work.

docs.title: Reporting under fan-out
docs.text: Per-sample fan-out makes one written step into many steps, and two things that were adequate for a single chain stop being adequate.

docs.title: An error carries its node, and its node's name — when the name is needed
docs.text:
CheckError gains node: Option<usize> and scope: Option<Scope>, both stamped by Graph::check and both None for a single step checked with check_step, which has nothing to distinguish it from itself.

pub struct Scope { pub kind: &'static str, pub value: String }

The scope goes in the heading — DimensionError in stepcall(sample SRR32217714): — rather than on a line of its own. The error shape M1 specified is step, both values, where each came from, a leading question; the sample says which step, so it belongs with the step.

It is added only where the step's own name is ambiguous. That condition is the whole of it, and getting it wrong in either direction is a bug:

  • A name belonging to one step needs nothing. docs/golden-example.md fixes the shape as in stepcall: and the project treats it as fixed, so a suffix identifying nothing a user was struggling to identify is noise on the commonest path — and the most common pipeline has no fan-out at all.
  • A name belonging to several needs something that tells those several apart. The sample is the right answer under fan-out. It is not the right answer for two same-named steps fed different alignments of one sample: both headings would read (sample sample_a), which looks exactly like an identifier while being none. That is the original bug in a smaller disguise.

So Graph::scopes groups the reachable step nodes by name, and for each name held by more than one node asks each Discriminator in turn for a value, taking the first that gives every node in the group a distinct one:

enum Discriminator { Sample, File }

Sample is the step's output sample set where it holds exactly one sample — or, where the output kind cannot carry one at all (an interval-producing step), the inputs, and only if every one that can speak to it names the same sample. A step spanning a whole cohort yields nothing, because labelling it after one of its samples would send a user to the wrong data.

File is the first file the node was built from, depth-first through the arguments in signature order, so a step two hops from any file still names the one its own first input came from.

If no discriminator separates the group, nothing is added. No suffix beats a misleading one.

Ambiguity is judged over the nodes being checked, not over the whole graph, so a twin built for a second pipeline in the same module does not start annotating this one's.

docs.title: The summary counts places, not names
docs.text:
summarise used to deduplicate the step names it saw, so four failing call nodes reported "4 errors in 1 step". That is not a cosmetic understatement: "1 step" describes a localised failure you fix by looking at one sample, and "4 steps" describes a cohort-wide one you fix by rethinking the pipeline. It now deduplicates on the node, falling back to the name when there is none.

The count is still of places rather than of errors, so one node with two problems correctly reads "2 errors in 1 step".

docs.title: One problem is stated once, and every sample is named
docs.text:
check::render groups errors whose text is identical once the scope is removed, prints the first in full, and adds one line naming the rest:

  The same problem affects 3 other samples: SRR32217715, SRR32217716, SRR32217726.

Named, not counted. A user who has to expand something to find out which samples failed has a shorter report rather than a better one, so every name is listed however many there are — four hundred accessions is a long line and four hundred identical paragraphs is an unusable report.

Two rules keep the collapsing honest:

  • An error that cannot name itself is never collapsed. With no scope there is nothing to put on the "also affects" line, so hiding one error behind an identical-looking one would leave a user unable to tell them apart. Those print separately.
  • A sample whose problem differs keeps its own paragraph. Grouping is on the full text of the problem, so a sample that failed for another reason can never be folded into the majority.

Collapsing is a property of the rendered report, not of the error list. Graph::check and pipe.errors() return one error per failing node, each with its own scope, because that is the granularity a program wants — counting affected samples, or retrying one of them.

docs.title: Intervals, and the order that is not an order
docs.text:
DataKind::Intervals was held back from M1 on purpose: the reference demo does not use intervals, and the coordinates dimension has nothing to do until they arrive, since SAM, BAM and VCF are all 1-based closed.

Parsing is hand-rolled, as FASTA is. Only the first column is needed, and noodles' BED reader is generic over the field count — materialising nine typed columns per record to read one of them would buy nothing and would put a pre-1.0 API in a hot loop. A GFF stops at ##FASTA, because a parser that kept going would report a contig named >chr1.

Contigs come from the records, so:

  • no length, no checksum. A BED records neither. Containment (D10) already compares only what is present, which is what makes these files checkable against a reference at all — by name, which catches a chr-prefixed BED against a bare reference and an interval on a contig the reference does not have. A GFF's ##sequence-region gives a length, but only when the region starts at base 1: a directive describing part of a contig says nothing about how long the contig is.
  • no dictionary order. This is the trap. relate compares the positions of matched contigs and reports OrderDiffers, because GATK requires sequence dictionaries to agree. A BED's records have an order too, but it is the order the intervals happen to be sorted in, and comparing it would report a contig order mismatch for a perfectly ordinary BED that lists contig 2 before contig 1.

So ReferenceId now records whether its contig list is a Dictionary or merely Observed, and order is compared only between two dictionaries.

docs.title: What intervals require
docs.text:
required_pair demands only coordinates of a pair involving intervals — never reference. An interval file's contigs come from its records, so an empty one knows none, and a user has no way to declare them: build= is a display label and cannot carry contigs. Requiring something nobody can supply is an unsatisfiable check, which the catalogue already treats as worse than a missed one (the same reasoning that keeps quality_encoding out of the table). It is still checked whenever both sides state it, which is every non-empty file.

coordinates, by contrast, is always known on both sides, because it is a property of the format. It is a demand the user can always satisfy and the one mismatch no amount of checksum comparison would catch.

docs.title: A miss this milestone fixed
docs.text:
Found while testing propagation, because the graph compares derived datasets with each other constantly where M1 mostly compared data against a reference.

Under Relation::Compatible — two datasets, neither of which is the reference — contigs the other side lacks are ignored. So a chr1-named VCF against a bare-named VCF shared nothing, agreed vacuously, and reported no error: there was nothing left in common to disagree about. The naming dimension did not catch it either, because naming is deliberately suppressed when both sides have a known reference, on the grounds that the reference comparison subsumes it.

A comparison pass that matched nothing can no longer claim agreement. It returns a third outcome, Disjoint, which is never reported and exists only to send the comparison into its second, normalised pass — where the overlap is found and the result is the naming error it always should have been. Two datasets that share nothing even normalised still agree, because a chr20-only VCF and a chr21-only VCF are both correct and saying otherwise would be a false alarm.

docs.title: Read pairing lives in Rust
docs.text:
lg.samples() globs in Python, with glob from the standard library, and groups in Rust. The split is not arbitrary: globbing is a filesystem convenience, while deciding that two files are mates of the same sample is correctness-critical. Pairing two samples' files by accident produces results for a mixture of two people and nothing crashes.

So a file whose mate cannot be identified is an error rather than a guess, a lone mate is an error rather than a single-end sample, and two files claiming the same mate is an error rather than a silent overwrite. The marker is matched anywhere in the stem rather than only at the end, and everything from it onwards is dropped, so Illumina's SAMPLE_R1_001.fastq.gz gives the sample SAMPLE rather than SAMPLE_001.

docs.title: The CLI is Python
docs.text:
ligase check has to import the user's pipeline module — that is how a Python pipeline declares itself, the way a Snakefile does — so it cannot be a Rust binary. argparse keeps it dependency-free.

The module is executed; the step bodies are not, because the decorator defers them. The acceptance test proves that rather than asserting it: every body in the test pipeline raises, so a passing check is evidence that nothing ran.

Pipelines are found by scanning the imported module's namespace for Pipeline instances. The alternative — a global registry that Pipeline writes itself into — would find pipelines built inside functions too, but at the cost of hidden global state that leaks between imports. Scanning requires the pipeline be assigned at the top level, which the error message says plainly.

The summary line is still worded in the core, so every surface reports a check the same way.

docs.title: Trade-offs and known gaps
docs.text:
• The handle is not really the type it claims to be. lg.handle() exists because of it, and a user who stores a step's output somewhere typed as Alignment and expects to read its contigs will find they must build the pipeline first. The payoff is static checking of pipeline wiring, which seems worth it.
  • Propagation picks the first stating input. Where two inputs disagree, the output takes one of them. The disagreement is reported at that step, so nothing is hidden, but a downstream error may name a value that came from the side you did not expect.
  • Plain parameters are recorded and otherwise ignored. min_freq is in the signature and in StepOutput.arguments, and does nothing until it joins the cache key (cache).
  • Nothing executes. pipe.run(), pipe.methods(), lg.sh() and ligase run are later milestones. The parser deliberately does not offer subcommands that would not work.
  • Requirements are still per-step at heart. The graph decides where to report a requirement and attributes it to its origin, but what counts as required still comes from required_pair over the kinds a step joins. A step cannot yet say "I need the sample set" on its own behalf.
  • One graph per pipeline. Two pipelines over the same inputs build two graphs and load nothing twice, but check the shared inputs twice over.
  • There are two discriminators, and a group gets one or none. A name shared by nodes that neither the sample nor a file separates is left unannotated, so those errors are reported separately rather than collapsed — correct, but less readable than it could be. Scope::kind is a &'static str so a third could be added.
  • Ambiguity is per check, so the same error can render two ways. Checking one pipeline where call is unique gives in stepcall:; checking a pipeline where it is not gives a suffix. That is the point, but it means the rendering of an error depends on the company it keeps.
