docs.text:
• Pipelines and the graph — the user-facing view
  • Type system architecture — dimensions, and the checker the graph drives
  • Decisions — D12, D13 and D14 were taken here

docs.title: Resistance interpretation, internally
docs.text:
Three layers in crates/ligase-core/src/hivdb/, none of which knows about Python:

Module Job ruleset read a vendored algorithm codon reference + VCF + BAM → the amino acids each protein holds score amino acids + algorithm → a level per drug report write the TSV

docs.title: The ruleset is derived, not parsed as XML
docs.text:
Stanford's algorithm is ASI2 XML, about 190 KB of it. Two files are committed per algorithm: that XML byte-for-byte, pinned by SHA-256 in rulesets/PROVENANCE.tsv, and a .ruleset derived from it by scripts/vendor_hivdb_algorithm.py.

The engine reads only the .ruleset, which means no XML parser in the core and no new dependency. The XML stays as the auditable thing you diff against upstream. tests/test_rulesets.py re-derives every .ruleset from its XML on every test run, so the two cannot drift apart unnoticed — a derived file that nothing re-derives is a file that can quietly stop matching its source.

The rulesets are then embedded with include_str!, so an installed wheel carries its own rules and a run cannot depend on where a file was unpacked. A test ties the embedded copy to the committed one.

docs.title: The grammar is small enough to be strict about
docs.text:
Every HIVDB release from 9.8 to 10.2 uses one shape:

SCORE FROM ( <item>, <item>, ... )

where an item is <residue> => <score>, several residues joined by AND, or MAX( several such ). There is no ATLEAST, NOTMORETHAN, SELECT or EXCLUDE; all 27 drugs use USE_GLOBALRANGE; and the global range is the same in both versions:

(-INF TO 9 => 1, 10 TO 14 => 2, 15 TO 29 => 3, 30 TO 59 => 4, 60 TO INF => 5)

So both the derivation and the reader refuse anything they do not recognise, rather than skipping it. That is D21's rule applied here: a reader that skipped what it did not understand would silently drop a drug, and a dropped drug reads as susceptible.

docs.title: The derived format
docs.text:
#ligase-hivdb-ruleset 1
algorithm   HIVDB   9.8   2025-01-05
level       1       S     Susceptible
range       *       9     1
gene        RT      NRTI,NNRTI
class       NRTI    ABC,AZT,D4T,DDI,FTC,3TC,TDF
drug        ABC     abacavir        NRTI
rule        ABC     2       45      65R
rule        ABC     21      10      65RN+151M

A rule row is drug, group, score, residues. Rows sharing a group are MAX alternatives; residues joined by + are the rule language's AND. A drug's score is the sum over groups of the largest matching item in each, which is exactly what SCORE FROM with MAX means.

Two details that matter:

  • A group with nothing matching contributes nothing, and the running maximum starts at None rather than at zero. Scores can be negative — 184V => -10 for zidovudine — and seeding at zero would silently turn a −10 into a 0.
  • Nothing is clamped. Stanford's own reports carry AZT -10.0 at level 1, and so does Ligase's.

docs.title: Amino acids are a bitset
docs.text:
Acids is a u32: bits 0–25 for A–Z, bit 26 for a deletion, bit 27 for an insertion, bit 28 for a stop codon. Matching a rule is then an intersection test, done once per rule position per drug per sample.

A stop codon can be observed but is never named by a rule, so it can never satisfy one — which is the right answer rather than a gap. A stop in the middle of protease is a defective virus, not a resistant one.

docs.title: Coverage, and the three states of a position
docs.text:
Protein holds only the positions that were read. A position read and agreeing with the reference is in it, holding the reference amino acid; a position with no coverage is absent. That absence is the whole mechanism:

State How What a rule does read, matches in the map, intersects the item matches read, does not match in the map, disjoint the item is refuted not read absent from the map the item is undetermined

An item is undetermined only when every residue that was read matches and at least one was not. An item already refuted by a read position is settled, so its unread positions are not reported — otherwise every drug would list most of its rule positions and the warning would mean nothing.

A gene absent from Observed altogether was never supplied, and its drugs come back Not assessed with no score.

docs.title: Codons
docs.text:
codon::GENES holds the HXB2 landmarks:

Gene HXB2 Codons CA 1186–1878 231 PR 2253–2549 99 RT 2550–4229 560 IN 4230–5093 288

Two of these were wrong in the demo before M6, and both errors were silent. Reverse transcriptase ran to 440 codons — the p51 subunit — where HIVdb numbers RT 1–560 and its published mutation lists reach 558. Integrase ran to 5096, which is where pol ends and includes its stop codon; the protein is 288 amino acids. hivdb_codons.rs now checks the windows against the rules, because a rule about a position outside the window would never fire and would do so quietly.

Reading a codon:

  1. Every base of the codon must be covered to depth, or the codon is left out. Two bases out of three is not two thirds of an amino acid.
  2. Each base's alleles are taken from the VCF's AD, keeping those at or above mixture. Every combination of them is a candidate.
  3. The reads decide which candidates are real. Reads spanning all three bases of the codon are counted as the triplets they carry, and the codon holds the amino acids whose share of those reads reaches mixture.

Step 3 is what D31 added, and step 2 is why it is needed: a VCF says what is at each position, not what travels together, so the candidates for a codon with two ambiguous bases include codons no read carries. All four used to be reported, which was six of M6's nine published discrepancies.

Three properties of step 3 are deliberate, and D31 argues each of them:

  • It only ever removes a candidate. Which alleles are present at a position stays the caller's quality-aware judgement.
  • The threshold is applied to the amino acid, summed over the triplets that spell it, not to each triplet on its own.
  • A codon the reads cannot settle — no read spanning it depth times, or no candidate among the reads at all — keeps its per-base reading, and Reading::notes says how many codons of which gene did that.

Reading::notes is a Vec<Note>, and the step hands it back to the engine rather than keeping it: write_report returns the notes, interpret_resistance returns them as the code-and-value pairs lg.write expects, and lg.hivdb.interpret's body returns those. From there the engine says them wherever it says what a run did (Notes). A reading made without an alignment, a gene nobody sequenced deeply enough and a codon no read spans are each a hedge with a clinical direction that the report file itself cannot state (D32).

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
codon::scan makes one pass over the BAM and answers both questions from the same bases: a dense u32 counter per gene position for coverage, and a dense [u32; 64] of triplet counts per codon, indexed by the triplet's place in the codon table. Dense because it is written once per codon per read — a few million times on a deep amplicon — and the whole table is a megabyte, which is cheaper to allocate once than to look a key up that often.

Reading sequences rather than spans roughly doubles the step: on the deepest run of the validation, 95,000 reads, resistance goes from 0.6s to 1.1s. It stays the cheapest step in the pipeline — half a second against an alignment that takes tens of them, and less than the demo's own run-to-run variation on the same code.

docs.title: How the rules reach the cache key
docs.text:
A callback step's recipe describes as the constant "callback", and code is the step function's source, not what a library it calls reads. So the rules had no home in a key at all.

They go in through tool=. That field already means "something whose version is part of the result", and its version string is already free-form — the whole of <tool> --version. exec::BUILT_IN, one entry long, makes the exception visible rather than hiding it inside the probe, and hivdb resolves to:

HIVdb rules as shipped: 9.8 2025-01-05 blake3:a1139c…; 10.2 2026-04-26 blake3:3268c9…

Three consequences, all deliberate:

  • By content, not by name. Upstream publishes corrections under near-identical names, so a key that moved only with the version number would serve a result computed under rules that have since changed.
  • Every shipped algorithm, not only the one in use, because the probe runs before any step body has said which it wants. Editing 10.2 reruns a pipeline pinned to 9.8. That is over-conservative in the direction D20 already commits to: a cache that is too cold costs time, one that is too warm is wrong.
  • "as shipped", because a methods paragraph renders a tool version after "ran with", and a step that named 9.8 must not appear to have run with 10.2. Which one a step used is its algorithm parameter, reported beside it.

Doing it this way also picks up provenance, the methods sentence and D24's citation table for free — and HIVdb genuinely needs a citation, which a plain parameter gave no home.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text:
Comments. Stanford's reports carry explanatory prose per mutation and per result. They are in the vendored XML, the derivation drops them, and Ligase reports levels, scores and mutations. They are the obvious addition if a report ever wants prose.

Any network call. Stanford's Sierra service appears in this repository exactly once: as the source of tests/fixtures/hivdb/expected.tsv, which was built once from published supplementary data and committed. Nothing queries it at run time or in CI.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
A note is a finding about one step's output that never changes a hash and never fails a run. It is carried beside the result into the run report, provenance, a reproducibility bundle and the methods section, so that every surface says the same thing in the same words.

The type lives in crates/ligase-core/src/note.rs. It used to live under canon/, and moved when the second producer arrived: a note is no longer something only canonicalisation finds.

docs.title: The type
docs.text:
pub enum Note {
    SampleIsAFile { sample: String },
    ReadingWithoutCoverage,
    GenePastReference { gene: String, end: u32, contig: String, length: u32 },
    GeneUnread { gene: String, depth: u32 },
    CodonsUnread { gene: String, read: u32, codons: u32, depth: u32 },
    CodonsUnphased { gene: String, unphased: u32, depth: u32 },
}

Closed, and spelled out, rather than a string. Each variant owns four things:

Method What it is for code() A stable kebab-case name, written into a cache, a provenance database and a bundle a reviewer may read next year. Spelled out per variant rather than derived from the enum, so renaming a variant cannot silently rename a stored code. value() What the note is about, as one column of a table. advice() What to do about it, in one line. Printed unwrapped beside a step's name in a terminal, so it is short. consequence() Why it matters, for a report with room to say so — the methods section and a bundle's README.

Display is the finding itself. Keeping all four beside the finding rather than in each report that prints one is what makes the run report, the bundle and the methods paragraph agree: there is only one copy of the wording.

docs.title: How a note with counts is stored
docs.text:
The cache, provenance and a bundle each keep a note as a code and one value, and Note::parse(code, value) has to be able to turn those back into the note — because the version that prints the sentence is not the one that found it. A note carrying counts therefore spells its fields out:

codons-unread    gene=RT read=220 codons=560 depth=100

Rather than storing the rendered sentence, which could not be reworded, and rather than storing the gene alone, which could not be worded at all. A value never contains a tab or a newline, since it is written into TSVs, and a value missing a field parse needs yields None — a half-read note is not a note.

Note::parse also returns None for a code this version does not know, so a store written by a later engine is read as far as it can be rather than rejected.

docs.title: Canonicalisation finds one in the file
docs.text:
canon::Digest::note collects notes while a file is being canonicalised, and Canonical carries them beside the hash. The rule and its three properties — a note never changes a hash, is dropped on the byte-fallback path, and collapses repeats — are in Canonicalisation.

These are stored against the hash of the output's bytes, in the cache's canonical table. That is the right key, because the finding is a fact about those bytes: the same file produced again by any route has the same note.

docs.title: A step says the other
docs.text:
The second kind cannot be found by reading an output at all. A resistance reading made without an alignment, and one made with full coverage, can write the same report; the assumption is visible only to the code that made it. So the body says it, through the door Host::call opens:

pub trait Host: Sync {
    fn call(
        &self,
        id: u64,
        out: &Path,
        inputs: &[(String, Vec<PathBuf>)],
    ) -> Result<Vec<Note>, String>;
}

A shell step always returns none: a command's assumptions are not something the engine can be told about.

In Python a lg.write body returns None, or pairs of a note's code and its value:

def produce(out: Path) -> list[Noticed]:
    return _core.interpret_resistance(reference.file, variants.file, str(out), ...)

return lg.write(produce)

interpret_resistance returns exactly those pairs, so the resistance step is a straight hand-back. The wording stays in Rust, which is the point: a body names the kind of note and what it is about, and the engine says the rest.

Two mistakes are refused rather than swallowed, because a note quietly dropped is the silence this door exists to end:

  • a code no Note names fails the step, naming the code;
  • a body that returns something other than notes is told what to return. The second is not hypothetical — lg.write(lambda out: out.write_text(…)) hands back a character count.

These notes are stored against the step's cache key, in a notes column on the steps table. Not against the output's hash, because they are not facts about those bytes — the whole reason they exist is that the bytes do not show them. The key does carry what they depend on: the alignment is an input, so a run with coverage and a run without have different keys.

docs.title: Where a note goes
docs.text:
Layer What it does with them cache::Entry notes, from the steps table, handed back on a cache hit. Cache::semantic The canonicalisation notes, from the canonical table. exec::StepResult One notes field holding both, the body's first. exec::noticed merges them without repeating any. exec::render A noticed line per note, with the advice stated once per kind (D15). prov::Record output_notes, in a produced_notes child table. prov::Methods A Noticed per node, gathered by step and kind by Methods::notices(), printed after the paragraph and the references. bundle A notes.tsv table and a What was noticed section in the README. StepRun.notes The Python surface: a tuple of sentences on every finished step.

Both kinds are stored rather than recomputed, and for the same reason. A cache hit neither reopens the file nor reruns the body, so a note that appeared on the first run and vanished on the second would be worse than no note at all.

That is the one cost. The cache's SCHEMA_VERSION moved to 3 for the new column, which clears its tables — D19 discards a cache from another version rather than migrating it, so there is nothing to write and nothing to lose. CANON_VERSION did not move, because nothing about what is hashed changed.

docs.title: What explains_a_difference is for
docs.text:
Bundle verification reports notes beside its verdicts, because a sample identifier that is a file is the second thing that explains a differs with no science behind it: such a hash depends on where the cache was.

A coverage hedge explains nothing of the kind. It is the same on every machine, and offering it as an excuse for a differs would send a reader after the wrong thing. So Note::explains_a_difference is true only for SampleIsAFile, and bundle::verify collects only those. Everything else still reaches the run report, notes.tsv, the README and the methods section — it is not a quieter note, just not an alibi.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: If you want to Read Know why the engine notices rather than refuses What a result rests on Read one, and fix it in a pipeline Reading what the engine noticed See the canonicalisation side Canonicalisation Read the decisions D26, D32

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
crates/ligase-core/src/prov/. No pyo3; exposed through ligase-py and reached from Python as pipe.methods() and ligase methods.

Three pieces, each answering a different question:

Module Question prov/mod.rs What was recorded about how a step ran? prov/methods.rs What would I write in a paper? prov/bundle.rs Would someone else get the same thing? prov/cite.rs Who do I credit for this tool?

docs.title: The store
docs.text:
provenance.sqlite, in the cache directory and not in cache.sqlite. One row per step key in produced, with four child tables — produced_parameters, produced_inputs, produced_references, produced_tools — rather than JSON blobs in one row, so that a question about a paper can be answered with sqlite3 and no parser:

$ sqlite3 .ligase/provenance.sqlite 'select tool, version from produced_tools'
minimap2|2.31-r1302
samtools|samtools 1.24...

That is the same bet the cache makes (D6), and it is why the engine needs no JSON library.

docs.title: Why a separate file
docs.text: Cache::open drops its tables when KEY_VERSION or CANON_VERSION moves, because an entry written under another format is a claim about ingredients that were combined differently and must never be read (D19). None of that reasoning applies to a record of what a command did. A separate file in the same directory survives every such bump for free, and PROV_VERSION tracks this schema on its own (D23).

docs.title: What is keyed, and what is not
docs.text:
A record is filed under the step key, which is already the identity of the computation: the same code, parameters, input contents and tool versions are the same step, and a second run of it has nothing new to say.

Two things are deliberately absent.

The scope. The sample label a report puts beside a step's name depends on the pipeline the step was reached from, not on the step. Graph::scopes can work it out whenever it is needed, and storing it would be a fact about one run masquerading as a fact about the computation.

Citations. A citation cannot change a result, so it is not a key ingredient — and storing one in a record would go stale the moment it was edited, since editing it does not rerun the step. prov::methods takes them from the pipeline in front of it, which is always current (D24).

docs.title: The write, and where it happens
docs.text:
In exec.rs, inside Runner::attempt, after the output is stored:

let produced = produce(&task.recipe, &inputs, &task.parameters, &staging, self.host)?;
// ...
self.remember(&Made { spec, task, key, inputs: &inputs,
                      command: produced.command, /* … */ })?;

It has to be there. exec::produce now returns an Execution carrying the command it ran, because fill_template is the only thing that ever renders it and the rendered command exists nowhere else — not in the cache, and since M4 not in the output either (D22).

A step served from the cache writes nothing. That is not an omission: the record from the run that did the work is still there, and that is the whole point of keeping it outside the cache.

Stores { cache, prov } is passed to exec::run and audit::audit so that "a run records provenance" is visible in the type rather than hidden in a constructor. A provenance write that fails fails the step, exactly as a cache metadata write already does: a result the engine cannot account for is not one it should serve.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
The hashes a record needs are the ones the key was just built from, so remember makes cache lookups rather than reads — the files prefilter and the memoised canonical table both answer from SQLite. One extra content_hash per input file is taken alongside the canonical hash, because a record names the file by its bytes as well as by its meaning.

Where that hashing happens matters more than what it costs. It runs inside the step's own worker, and BLAKE3 hashes a large file across whatever thread pool it is called from — so writing a record, like building a key, queues work on the executor's own pool. That is safe only because no worker in that pool is ever blocked waiting for scheduler work (D27, the scheduler). A ligase methods run on the demo is what found this out, by hanging.

docs.title: Pinning a reference
docs.text:
prov::pin reads ReferenceId, which load::reference already filled:

  • accession — the contig name, where it looks like one. The check is is_accession: one to six uppercase letters, an optional underscore, five to ten digits, an optional .version. K03455.1 and NC_001802.1 pass; chr1 and 1 do not.
  • checksum — the per-contig MD5 the loader computes over the uppercased sequence with whitespace removed, which is the digest the SAM specification prescribes for @SQ M5 (D11). It is given for a single-sequence reference; a multi-sequence one has no single checksum to name.
  • fingerprint — always present, so a reference with no accession is still told apart from any other.

Nothing here is declared, and nothing is guessed. That is the whole reason the accession requirement cost no new API: both halves of "accession plus checksum" were already being read off the file in M1.

docs.title: The paragraph
docs.text: prov::methods takes a graph, its roots, the tasks, a run report and the store. The run report is where the keys come from, which is why pipe.methods() runs the pipeline first.

docs.title: Grouping
docs.text:
One written step becomes one node per sample, and four identical sentences with a different accession in each would be unreadable. So nodes are grouped by a signature of everything that could make their sentences differ — step name, command template, parameters, tool versions, reference fingerprints — and each group gets one sentence saying how many nodes it covers.

Where two nodes of a step genuinely were run differently they fall into different groups and get a sentence each. That is not a special case; it is the same rule, and it puts the difference in front of the reader.

docs.title: Wording
docs.text:
Fixed sentence forms, assembled in Group::sentence and wrapped at 76 columns. Two details worth knowing:

  • describe_tool does not say a tool's name twice. samtools --version prints samtools 1.24, while minimap2 --version prints 2.31-r1302 and nothing else, so the name is prepended only when the version does not already start with it. Only the first line reaches a sentence; the rest — the htslib a samtools was built against — is in the bundle.
  • The template is printed, not the filled command. A filled command names a staging file inside the cache, which is true and of no use in a paper. The filled one is in the record, and commands.tsv prints it.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text: A node whose key has no record becomes a Gap, reported by name with ligase run --force as the remedy. Nothing can reconstruct such a command, which is exactly the trade D22 made.

docs.title: The bundle
docs.text:
prov::bundle::write takes a Request and produces a directory. Seven flat TSV tables, the source of every step, whatever files the caller asked to carry along (the CLI passes the pipeline file), and a MANIFEST hashing all of it with BLAKE3.

Fields are escaped — \\, \t, \n, \r — so a command containing a tab cannot shift a column, and unescape reads them back.

docs.title: What "a clean machine" means
docs.text: A bundle cannot carry the reference pipeline's inputs: they are gigabytes, and fetching them is out of scope (D8). So the claim is narrower and checkable: a run with these inputs, on a machine with these tools, lands on these canonical hashes. To this engine a clean machine is an empty cache — nothing computed, nothing remembered, every tool probed again — and that is what the acceptance test uses (D25).

docs.title: The four verdicts
docs.text:
verify matches the bundle's rows to a fresh run's results by (step, scope) rather than by key, because the key is the thing that may legitimately have moved:

Verdict Key Result Identical same same Reproduced different same Differs either different Missing — this pipeline produced nothing for it

Reproduced is the verdict that justifies the whole mechanism. Keys are content-addressed, so a bundle checked on a machine with the same data and the same tool versions comes out Identical — and one checked where the aligner is a different build comes out Reproduced, which is a stronger statement than the cache could ever make.

Inputs are checked by content as well, and reported only when something moved: a run of four hundred samples should not print four hundred lines to say nothing changed.

docs.title: The citation table
docs.text: Four entries' worth of promise: minimap2 (Li 2018) and samtools / bcftools (Danecek et al. 2021, one paper for both). It is short on purpose — every entry is a commitment to keep a reference correct, and a long list of half-checked citations is worth less than a short list of checked ones plus an honest gap. Anything else comes from cite= on the step, and a tool neither covers is named as uncited.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text:
Validation. Whether the resistance calls agree with the published ones is M6. Provenance says how a number was produced; it says nothing about whether it is right.

Fetching pinned data. A bundle names its inputs by content hash and its references by accession and checksum, and checks the ones it finds. Going and getting them is out of scope for v0.1 (D8).

A history of runs. One row per step key, replaced if the same key is produced again. The key is the computation, so the second run has nothing new to say about it except the machine and the moment, where the later answer is the better one. A pipeline wanting an append-only log of every invocation would want a different table, not a different key.

A repair for a tool that names a sample after a file. bcftools names a VCF's sample column after its input BAM's path when the BAM carries no @RG SM, and a Ligase run hands it a path inside the content-addressed store. The canonical form of a VCF includes its sample names — correctly, because a sample set is a dimension — so such a VCF's canonical hash depends on where the cache is, and a bundle written from one cache cannot verify against another. Bundle verification is what found it.

The engine now notices this and says so, in the run report, in the record, in notes.tsv and in the methods section (D26, canonicalisation). What it does not do is fix it, and will not: refusing the file would make a format problem into an engine failure in the layer D21 forbids it, and rewriting the identifier would be a silent repair that does not even work — a file in the store is named after the hash of its bytes, which move with the cache root too. The fix is one line in the pipeline, and align in the reference pipeline has it.

Provenance for a step that failed. pipe.methods() refuses a pipeline with a failure rather than describing the steps that worked, because a paragraph covering most of a pipeline reads exactly like a paragraph covering all of it.

docs.title: Type system architecture
docs.text: How dimension checking is built, and why it is built this way. The user-facing view is Types and dimensions.

docs.title: Where the code lives
docs.text:
crates/ligase-core/src/
  dim/mod.rs        Source, Dim<T>, Dimension, Dimensions, and the value types
  dim/reference.rs  Contig, ReferenceId, and the relation between references
  types.rs          DataKind, Dataset, and the applicability matrix
  check.rs          check_step, the requirements table, error rendering
  load/fasta.rs     streaming FASTA scan with computed MD5
  load/alignment.rs SAM and BAM headers
  load/variants.rs  VCF headers
  load/reads.rs     FASTQ pairing, quality encoding, grouping into samples
  load/intervals.rs BED and GFF records

crates/ligase-py/src/lib.rs   thin PyO3 translation, no logic
python/ligase/__init__.py     loaders, exception hierarchy, docstrings
python/ligase/types.py        Dataset and its per-kind subclasses

All correctness-critical logic is in ligase-core, which has no PyO3 dependency and can be tested and fuzzed as an ordinary Rust crate. The binding layer translates and nothing more; in particular, error wording is generated in Rust so the Rust tests own it, and asserting on exact message text does not require a Python round trip.

docs.title: Provenance lives in the value
docs.text:
pub enum Dim<T> {
    Known { value: T, source: Source },
    Unknown { reason: &'static str },
}

pub enum Source {
    Inferred { path: PathBuf, detail: &'static str },
    Declared,
    Derived { step: String },
}

The alternative — storing bare values and reconstructing provenance when an error is built — was rejected. Reconstruction means the error site has to re-derive which file a value came from, which is guesswork once values have been propagated through a graph. Storing it costs one PathBuf per dimension and makes the error site trivial.

Unknown carries a reason rather than being a bare None, because "unknown" is a thing the user has to act on and the reason is the instruction: "no @RG lines with an SM tag in the header" tells them what to look at, where None tells them nothing.

docs.title: Reference identity
docs.text:
pub struct Contig {
    pub name: String,
    pub length: Option<u64>,
    pub md5: Option<String>,
}

pub struct ReferenceId { label: Option<String>, contigs: Vec<Contig> }

label is display only and never participates in comparison. length is optional because ##contig=<ID=1> without a length is legal VCF; storing a zero there would be a value that compares equal to another lie. md5 is optional because VCF ##contig lines frequently omit it and FASTQ has no concept of one.

Two contigs are the same contig when their normalised names match, their lengths agree if both are recorded, and their checksums agree if both are recorded. Comparing only what is present is the honest middle between refusing to compare at all (which makes VCFs uncheckable) and treating an absent digest as agreement (which is the lie this whole system guards against).

docs.title: Name normalisation
docs.text:
A leading chr is stripped, case-insensitively, because naming style is its own dimension. A stripped M then becomes MT, reconciling UCSC's chrM with Ensembl's MT.

The alias applies only to the prefixed form. A bare M is left alone, so it does not silently equate to MT. This is not fussiness: hg19's chrM is the older NC_001807 at 16571 bp, while GRCh37's MT is the rCRS at 16569 bp. They are different sequences. Normalising the name is safe only because length and MD5 are still compared, and the narrow alias keeps the one case that is genuinely the same contig from needing a special case.

docs.title: The relation, and why it is not equality
docs.text:
pub enum Relation {
    Identical,   // two references compared with each other
    DataWithin,  // data checked against a reference
    Compatible,  // two datasets, neither of which is the reference
}

Decision D10. Strict equality everywhere was the first design and it is wrong: a VCF header routinely lists only the contigs it has variants on, so ##contig=<ID=chr20> against whole-genome hg38 is correct input that equality rejects.

Rejecting correct input is not a safe failure. It teaches users to work around check(), and a bypassed checker catches nothing. So data need only be contained in the reference, while two references compared with each other must still match exactly.

Orientation follows the kinds, not the argument order — data is checked against a reference, never the reverse — so the relation is the same however the bindings happen to be listed.

docs.title: Classifying a failure
docs.text:
relate compares twice: once on the names as written, and if that fails, once on normalised names.

raw comparison agrees                     -> Agree
raw fails, normalised agrees              -> NamingDiffers
otherwise, report the normalised verdict  -> MissingContig | ContigConflict | OrderDiffers

A failure that becomes a success under normalisation is a naming difference. That two-pass structure is what makes chr1 against 1 a distinct error rather than a reference mismatch, and it generalises to containment for free.

OrderDiffers is its own verdict rather than being folded into a reference mismatch or ignored. htslib matches contigs by name, so bcftools does not care — but GATK requires sequence dictionaries in matching order and will reject the input. Reporting it as a reference mismatch would misdirect; staying silent would hide a real failure.

docs.title: Fingerprints
docs.text:
ReferenceId::fingerprint() is a 12-hex-character MD5 over the canonical contig list, used for display only, when two references' human descriptions collide. Two files both labelled hg38 must not render identically in an error message.

It is computed over normalised names, so a reference fingerprints the same as its chr-prefixed twin — naming is a separate dimension and must not leak into identity.

docs.title: Checked against required
docs.text:
This is the central design decision of the checker.

// Checked:  both sides state a value -> they must agree. Every dimension.
// Required: additionally, the value must not be unknown. Only these pairs:
pub const fn required_pair(left: DataKind, right: DataKind) -> &'static [Dimension]
Kinds joined Must be known Reference ↔ Reference / Alignment / Variants reference Alignment ↔ Alignment reference Alignment ↔ Variants, Variants ↔ Variants reference, sample_set Reads ↔ Reads sample_set, pairing Reads ↔ Alignment / Variants sample_set Reads ↔ Reference nothing Intervals ↔ anything but Reads coordinates Reads ↔ Intervals nothing anything ↔ ResistanceReport nothing

docs/dimensions.md says unknown dimensions are allowed only if no downstream step requires them. Checking one step in isolation has no downstream, so check_step takes "required" from the kinds being joined. A whole pipeline does have one: the graph uses disagreements() and requires() to decide for itself, attributing a gap to the input that has to declare it, and this table is its default.

Three entries deserve their reasoning spelled out:

  • Reads ↔ Reference requires nothing. Introducing the reference is what alignment does. The golden example's lg.samples() takes no organism, and demanding one would break a documented API for no safety gain.
  • organism is required nowhere. Reference identity already implies it: if two inputs agree on contig checksums, they agree on the organism. Requiring a declaration would add a hurdle without adding safety. It is still checked when both sides state one.
  • quality_encoding is required nowhere. The catalogue gives no way to declare it, so requiring it would be an unsatisfiable check — the user could not comply.
  • reference is required nowhere for intervals. The same reasoning. A BED's contigs come from its records, so an empty one knows none and build= is a display label that cannot carry contigs. coordinates is required instead: it is a property of the format, so it is always known and always satisfiable.

The bias throughout is toward demanding less. Under-demanding loses a check that another dimension usually catches anyway; over-demanding produces false alarms, and false alarms are how a correctness tool gets switched off.

docs.title: The applicability matrix
docs.text:
DataKind::applies(Dimension) -> bool encodes the n/a cells of the catalogue table. A dimension outside a kind's set is never compared and never demanded.

This keeps "does not apply" genuinely distinct from "unknown", which matters for the error messages: check_step should never ask a user to declare a FASTA's quality encoding.

Alignment reports pairing as applicable but unknown, because the information is in the SAM flags and M1 reads headers only. The unknown reason says exactly that rather than falling back to a generic one.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
pub struct CheckError {
    kind: ErrorKind,      // Dimension | ContigNaming | ContigOrder | Undeclared
    step: String,
    dimension: Dimension,
    lines: Vec<String>,   // one per binding
    detail: Option<String>,
    conclusion: String,
}

lines is pre-rendered free-form text rather than structured values, because the three error shapes genuinely differ: a dimension mismatch reads aln.reference = HXB2 (...), an order mismatch reads aln.reference lists contigs in the order 2, 1 (...), and an undeclared dimension reads aln.organism is unknown (...).

Two rendering details that are easy to get wrong:

  • Naming and order lines are rendered from each binding's own dimensions rather than from the verdict's left/right. The verdict is oriented by kind while the lines are ordered by binding, so reading the styles off the verdict would eventually mislabel which file had which naming style.
  • The preposition belongs to the Source, not the template around it: describe() returns "from BAM @SQ header: path" but plain "declared", because "(from declared)" does not read as English.

The undeclared message puts the unknown side first regardless of binding order, because that is the side the user has to change.

check_step returns every error rather than the first. ligase check has to report all type errors in one pass, and fixing errors one per overnight run is the problem Ligase exists to remove. The Python check_step raises the first but attaches all of them to .errors; dimension_errors returns the list without raising.

dimension is an Option<Dimension>. A StepType error — a step handed a VCF where it declared a FASTA — blames no dimension, and storing one anyway would mean choosing a lie for the Python layer to report.

docs.title: FASTA is hand-rolled
docs.text:
noodles is used for SAM, BAM, VCF and FASTQ, but not FASTA. Its FASTA reader materialises each record's sequence, and a human reference is three gigabases — a loader that held each contig in memory to checksum it would need gigabytes of RAM to answer a question about a header.

The replacement is a ~60-line streaming scan that updates an MD5 and a length counter line by line and holds no sequence at all. It also handles the canonical form the M5 checksum is defined over: uppercased, whitespace stripped, so soft-masked repeats do not change a reference's identity.

docs.title: Gzip is read with a multi-member decoder
docs.text: flate2::bufread::MultiGzDecoder, never the single-member decoder. BGZF — the block-gzip that bgzip, samtools and bcftools produce — is a sequence of gzip members, and a single-member decoder stops silently after the first block. That failure mode is reading the start of a file and believing it to be all of it, which is exactly the class of silent wrongness this project targets.

docs.title: ##reference is deliberately ignored
docs.text: A VCF's ##reference holds a path or URL. docs/dimensions.md is explicit that reference identity never rests on a filename, so identity comes from ##contig alone and a VCF with no ##contig lines reports its reference as unknown rather than trusting the path.

docs.title: @SQ SP is not a source for organism
docs.text:
The SAM specification has a species tag, and reading it would be easy. It is deliberately unused: matching a free-text "Homo sapiens" against a declared "human" needs an alias table, and a wrong answer there passes check() silently. Organism on a BAM is unknown unless declared.

Organism comparison itself normalises case and surrounding whitespace and nothing else. No alias table, documented as such, so users declare one spelling and use it.

docs.title: Quality encoding is bounded and may abstain
docs.text:
Up to 10 000 records are sampled. Any byte below 59 means Phred+33 definitively (no 64-offset encoding can produce it) and the scan stops early; a maximum above 74 means Phred+64. Anything else returns unknown.

The bound means a file whose only distinguishing scores appear late reports unknown — the safe direction to be wrong in. Guessing would shift every quality value by 31, and nothing downstream would notice.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Format fixtures live in crates/ligase-core/tests/fixtures/, generated by a committed generate.py so they are reproducible and so the MD5s baked into the @SQ M5 and ##contig md5 fields are derived rather than hand-typed. Running it on an unchanged tree rewrites the same bytes, so git diff --exit-code after running it checks that the fixtures match the generator.

Fixtures are committed as text — SAM, VCF, FASTA, FASTQ — so a reviewer can read an @SQ M5 and check it by hand. BAM, being binary, is written at test time from a committed SAM's header. That keeps binaries out of git while leaving the text fixture as the source of truth: a BAM test is not merely noodles' writer agreeing with noodles' reader about a header neither was given.

Because data/ is gitignored, anything touching real data skips when absent rather than failing in CI. Two tests do:

  • the real HXB2 FASTA, after scripts/fetch_test_data.sh
  • the real minimap2 alignment, after scripts/make_demo_alignment.sh

That second script rebuilds the BAM header with samtools dict so the @SQ lines carry M5 checksums. minimap2 does not write them, and without them a reference check falls back to names and lengths — the weak check Ligase exists to replace, since hg19 and hg38 share plenty of both. The payoff is that the test verifies a checksum we computed from the FASTA against one samtools computed independently, on a header a real aligner produced.

docs.title: Trade-offs and known gaps
docs.text:
• noodles is pre-1.0. It bumps minor versions often and its MSRV sets ours (currently Rust 1.91). The alternative, rust-htslib, needs a C htslib at build time, which would break pip install ligase-bio on any machine without one. See D11.
  • Contig order is compared strictly even for a contained subset. Tools differ on whether they care; reporting it separately lets a caller decide, but a pipeline that legitimately reorders will see an error it must handle.
  • Contig order is only compared between dictionaries. ReferenceId records whether its contigs came from a sequence dictionary or were merely observed in records, and Observed lists are never compared for order. See the graph.
  • No conversion graph yet. check_step reports a mismatch; it does not search for a liftover or a renaming step that would fix it. That is v2, by D5 and D8.
  • Organism aliases are not resolved. human and Homo sapiens are different strings and will be reported as a mismatch if both are declared. Deliberate, per the reasoning above, but it is a rough edge.

docs.title: Workspace architecture
docs.text: How the M0 scaffold is wired, and what each choice costs.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
Cargo.toml                 workspace root: shared version, lints, deps
├── crates/ligase-core/    [package] name = "ligase"   -- the engine
└── crates/ligase-py/      [lib] name = "_core"        -- cdylib bindings
pyproject.toml             maturin backend, dist "ligase-bio"
python/ligase/             python-source root

One version number lives in [workspace.package] and everything inherits it with version.workspace = true. The Python distribution takes it too, via dynamic = ["version"], which maturin fills from the crate it builds. There is exactly one place to bump a release, and no way for the Rust and Python halves to disagree.

That last part is tested rather than assumed:

def test_version_matches_workspace_manifest() -> None:
    import ligase
    assert ligase.__version__ == workspace_version()   # parsed from Cargo.toml


def test_core_version_comes_from_rust() -> None:
    import ligase
    assert ligase._core.version() == ligase.__version__

The second test is the one that matters. It would still pass if __version__ were hardcoded to the right string — so it is paired with the first, which reads the manifest. Together they fail if the Python package reports a version the engine was not built from.

docs.title: The build
docs.text:
maturin is the PEP 517 backend. The relevant configuration:

[tool.maturin]
manifest-path = "crates/ligase-py/Cargo.toml"
module-name = "ligase._core"
python-source = "python"

This is maturin's mixed layout: a hand-written Python package with a compiled module dropped inside it. python-source = "python" tells maturin the package root is python/, and module-name places the shared object at python/ligase/_core.abi3.so. The result is that pip install -e . produces one importable ligase whose __init__.py you can edit without rebuilding, containing a _core you cannot.

docs.title: abi3
docs.text:
The bindings build against abi3-py311 — Python's stable ABI, from 3.11 onwards. One compiled artifact works on 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 and later.

The cost is real: abi3 closes off parts of the CPython C API, so some PyO3 features are unavailable, and a #[pyclass] under abi3 is marginally slower than a version-specific build. We accept that. The alternative is a build matrix with one wheel per Python version per platform, which multiplies CI time and release surface by four or five. For a project whose hot path will be hashing files and shelling out to aligners, the per-call overhead of a stable-ABI class is not where the time goes.

The floor is 3.11 rather than 3.10 for two reasons: 3.10 reaches end of life in October 2026, and tomllib is in the standard library from 3.11, which the version test uses to read Cargo.toml without a dependency.

docs.title: Why the engine has no pyo3 dependency
docs.text:
ligase-core does not depend on pyo3 at all; ligase-py depends on both. This is enforced by the manifests rather than by discipline.

The payoff is that the engine's test suite is plain cargo test with no Python interpreter in the loop, which keeps the inner development loop fast and means a type error in the engine surfaces in milliseconds. It also keeps the engine usable from Rust, which matters for the conversion graph in v2.

The cost is a translation layer that must be written by hand, and the temptation to let types leak across it for convenience. The leading underscore on _core is the reminder that the layer is allowed to change.

docs.title: Lints as rules
docs.text:
CLAUDE.md says "no unwrap outside tests". Rather than leaving that to code review, the workspace makes it a build error:

[workspace.lints.clippy]
unwrap_used = "deny"
expect_used = "deny"

[workspace.lints.rust]
missing_docs = "warn"

missing_docs is a warning locally and an error in CI, where clippy runs with -D warnings. So an undocumented public item fails the build — the documentation rule, applied to code.

Test files opt out explicitly, at the top of the file:

#![allow(clippy::unwrap_used, clippy::expect_used)]

That is the point of the design. An unwrap in a test is fine and an unwrap in the engine is not, and the opt-out is visible in the diff when someone adds a file that needs it.

docs.title: Trade-offs taken
docs.text:
One repository, not three. The engine, the bindings and the Python package version and release together. A scientist installing Ligase should never have to reason about which engine version their Python package wants. The cost is that the Rust crate's releases are coupled to the Python package's, which would matter if other Rust programs depended on ligase — none do yet.

Source distribution only, for now. Installing needs a Rust toolchain, which is a real barrier for the target user. Pre-built wheels via maturin-action are the fix, and belong with the first release rather than with the scaffold; publishing wheels for a package that cannot yet check a pipeline would be premature.

ruff does not see docs/. Recent ruff formats Python inside fenced Markdown blocks, which means it wants to reformat the golden example — adding blank lines between decorated functions and de-aligning its comments. That document is the specification the engine is built to satisfy, and its shape is deliberate, so extend-exclude = ["docs"] keeps the formatter out of it. The trade is that example code in the docs is not machine-checked. Once the API exists, the right fix is doctests that actually run, not a formatter that rewrites prose.

Four CI jobs, eight job-runs. The Python gate runs on 3.11 and 3.14 across Linux and macOS. abi3 means the compiled artifact is not version-specific, so the matrix is really testing that the build works across interpreters and platforms, not the extension's behaviour on each. Two versions at the ends of the supported range catch that; testing all four would buy very little.

docs.title: What M0 deliberately leaves out
docs.text:
No dimension types, no graph, no cache, no execution. The only behaviour the engine has is reporting its own version.

Dependencies were kept to the minimum that a scaffold needs: pyo3 and nothing else. blake3, rusqlite and rayon arrive with the milestones that need them, and the BAM and VCF header parsing that M1 requires will need a format library — noodles being the obvious candidate. Adding them now would mean guessing at an interface before the thing that uses it exists.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Project layout — the three layers and why
  • Installation — the developer loop
  • Decisions — D1 on the Rust/Python split, D4 on canonicalisation

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
pipe.run() computes whatever is not already known. A step runs when something that could change its result has changed, and not otherwise:

$ ligase run examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py
running 12 steps in examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py

ran       `align` (sample SRR8525904)        4.5s
ran       `call` (sample SRR8525904)         513ms
ran       `resistance` (sample SRR8525904)   3ms
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525908)        9.4s
...

12 steps: 12 ran.

Run it again and nothing happens, because nothing changed:

$ ligase run examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py
running 12 steps in examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py

cached    `align` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942
cached    `call` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942
cached    `resistance` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942

12 steps: 12 from cache.

Eleven seconds became two tenths of one. The interesting part is not the speed; it is that the second run is entitled to be that fast, and can say why.

docs.title: What a step's identity is
docs.text:
Every step gets a key:

hash(function code, parameters, input content hashes, tool versions)

If the key is in the cache, the step does not run. That list is exactly the set of things that can change a step's result, and the words in it are chosen carefully.

Function code, not a name. Editing a step's body reruns it. Renaming a file does not.

Parameters, by value and by type. min_freq=0.01 and min_freq=0.05 are different steps; so are 0.01 and "0.01", because a framework that hashed them the same would be guessing. A random seed is an ordinary parameter, which is why a seed has to be declared rather than drawn: a step that reaches for an unseeded random number is not reproducible, and no cache can make it so.

Input content hashes, never timestamps (D2). Timestamps lie. cp moves them, git clone moves them, touch moves them, and a restored backup moves them backwards. A pipeline that reran on a fresh checkout — or worse, did not rerun after a file was quietly replaced — would be a pipeline nobody trusts.

Tool versions. @lg.step(tool="bcftools") is not decoration: the step's key includes what bcftools --version says. Two bcftools releases that disagree about a call are precisely the reproducibility failure this project exists to catch, so an upgrade reruns the steps it could have changed. A tool that is not installed is an error, not an empty string, because hashing an absent tool as "no version" would let two machines with different tools agree on a key.

docs.title: Why outputs are named after their contents
docs.text:
A finished output goes into a content-addressed store: its name is the BLAKE3 hash of its bytes. Two steps that produced identical results share one file between them, and an object's name is a claim about its contents that anyone can check.

That is also what makes early cutoff fall out rather than being bolted on. A downstream key is built from its inputs' contents, so if a step reruns and produces the same bytes as before, every key below it is unchanged and nothing below it is redone:

$ ligase run pipeline.py      # after a comment-only edit to `align`
ran       `align`   17ms
skipped   `call`

2 steps: 1 ran, 1 skipped.

align reran — its code changed, and the cache is not in the business of deciding which edits matter. But its output did not change, so call had nothing to do. The report distinguishes the two cases on purpose: cached means nothing above it ran, skipped means something did and came out the same.

"The same" means scientifically the same, not byte-identical: semantic hashing sorts an output's records and drops the fields that say when and how it was made before hashing it. With bytes the example above would not work at all on a real aligner, because minimap2 writes its own command line — including the output path — into the BAM's @PG line.

docs.title: Why every sample is its own work
docs.text:
One written step becomes one step per sample (per-sample fan-out), and each of those gets its own key. So adding a sample to a cohort of four hundred is three new steps rather than twelve hundred:

$ ligase run pipeline.py      # one more sample arrived
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525942)        8.2s
ran       `call` (sample SRR8525942)         430ms
ran       `resistance` (sample SRR8525942)   0ms
cached    `align` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920
cached    `call` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920
cached    `resistance` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920

12 steps: 3 ran, 9 from cache.

Independent samples also run at once, at whatever width the machine allows. Nothing special makes that true: samples have no edges between them, so the engine has nothing to serialise.

docs.title: What the cache cannot see
docs.text:
Two honest limitations, both worth knowing before trusting a result.

A file rewritten in place. Hashing every input on every run would make a 40 GB BAM expensive to look at, so a file whose size and modification time are unchanged is not read again (D3). Note the shape of that bet: a match skips work, a mismatch only causes a rehash, and the hash itself is never taken from a timestamp. The one case it can miss is a file edited in place, keeping its exact length, within the same timestamp granularity. --force exists for it.

A step that lies about what it reads. A command that opens a file no parameter mentions has an input the key knows nothing about. Ligase cannot see inside bcftools; it can only hash what the step says it uses. This is the same bargain every build system makes, and the reason steps declare their inputs as parameters rather than reaching for paths.

docs.title: Where it all goes
docs.text:
A single directory, .ligase/, under wherever you ran from:

.ligase/
├── cache.sqlite          what has been computed, and what it produced
├── store/                outputs, named after the hash of their contents
│   └── 3c/73431de6...eeaa85.tsv
└── tmp/                  steps write here, before the store knows them

It is derived data, all of it: delete the directory and the next run recomputes. Keep it and the next run is instant. It belongs in .gitignore, which is where this project's own is.

docs.text:

  • Cache architecture — the store, the schema, and how a key is actually composed.
  • Execution architecture — how a graph becomes parallel work without Python in the hot path.

docs.title: What a result rests on
docs.text:
A run can succeed and still have something worth saying about what it produced. That is a note: a statement about an output that its hash cannot carry, printed beside the result and never instead of it. A note is not an error. The step ran, its output is in the store, and the run succeeded.

Two things put one there, and they look for different kinds of trouble.

  • Reading the output finds a field that cannot be dropped and is still wrong — a sample identifier that is a file name rather than a sample.
  • The step that wrote it says what its work rested on, which no reading of the file could recover: a resistance reading made without coverage takes every position the caller did not report to be reference, and the report it writes looks exactly like one that had full coverage.

Both end up in the same place, because to a reader they are the same question: what should I know about this result that the number does not say?

docs.title: The field that cannot be dropped
docs.text:
Ligase drops a great deal from a file before hashing it. The command line minimap2 records, the timestamp bcftools writes beside its own — none of that is a result, so none of it is part of what a file means. The rule that makes this safe is simple: drop what says when and how a file was made, keep what says what is in it.

Some fields fall on the wrong side of that line and are still wrong.

A VCF names its samples on the #CHROM line, in the columns the genotypes line up with:

#CHROM  POS  ID  REF  ALT  QUAL  FILTER  INFO  FORMAT  SRR8525904

That is not how the file was made. It is what the file is about — a sample set is one of the four dimensions this engine exists to keep straight, and dropping it would mean two VCFs of two different patients hashing the same. So it stays in the hash.

Now run bcftools on an alignment that carries no read group:

#CHROM  POS  ID  ...  FORMAT  /Users/kelyn/ligase/.ligase/store/62/7db9fa0cbac.bam

With no @RG SM to read, bcftools names the sample column after the input file's path — and the input file, in a Ligase run, lives inside the content-addressed store. The calls now carry a cache path where a sample identifier belongs.

docs.title: Why that is worse than untidy
docs.text:
The hash of that VCF now depends on where the cache directory is. Two machines running the same pipeline on the same data produce calls that are byte-identical in every variant record and disagree on the one line that is hashed. A reproducibility bundle written on one of them cannot verify on the other: every sample comes back differs, with nothing scientific behind it.

That is exactly how this was found. M5's bundle verification reported differs on every sample of the reference pipeline, and the whole of the difference was the last column of one line.

It is also wrong in two quieter ways. A generated methods paragraph names a cache path where it should name a run accession. And the sample-set dimension — the thing that is supposed to catch shuffled sample IDs — is holding a file name, so it cannot catch anything.

docs.title: So the engine says what it saw
docs.text:
Ligase does not drop the identifier, because a sample set is a dimension. It does not rewrite it either, because silently repairing a wrong file is how a pipeline comes to produce plausible numbers nobody can account for — and in this case the repair would not even work.

Why not just use the basename?

Reducing /…/store/62/7db9fa0cbac.bam to 7db9fa0cbac looks like it would make the hash portable. It would not. A file in the store is named after the hash of its bytes, and an alignment's bytes contain the staging path samtools sort -o recorded — which is inside the cache. The basename moves with the cache root exactly as the whole path does. It would also collapse two genuinely different samples whose file names agree.

What the engine does instead is notice, and tell you (D26):

$ ligase run
ran       `call` (sample SRR8525904)   513ms

noticed   `call` (sample SRR8525904): the sample identifier `/Users/kelyn/ligase/.ligase/store/62/7db9fa0cbac.bam` is an absolute path, not a sample
          Write the read group — `samtools addreplacerg -r ID:<sample> -r SM:<sample>` — so the calls below it name the sample.

4 steps: 4 ran.

A note is not an error. The step ran, its output is there, and the run succeeded. It is a statement about something the hash cannot express, and it travels with the result: into the run report, into the provenance record, into the bundle and into the generated methods section. The fix is one line in the pipeline, and it is a line only you can write.

docs.title: Why nothing louder
docs.text:
Refusing the file would be the obvious loud answer, and it is the wrong layer for it. A VCF whose sample column holds a path is perfectly valid VCF; canonicalisation has no business failing a run over a file that parses (D21).

Refusing it at ligase check time is loud and ineffective, which is worse. The checker runs before any compute, so the only files it can see are inputs — and the file with the wrong identifier is an output of the step below. A check-time rule would have missed the failure that prompted all of this, and fired only on hand-supplied files that are not wrong.

docs.title: What counts as a file
docs.text:
Narrowly, because a rule that guessed would report good identifiers as mistakes and a warning nobody trusts gets ignored. An identifier is a file when it:

  • holds a path separator — / or \ — or
  • ends in an extension naming a format this engine reads: .bam, .cram, .sam, .vcf, .bcf, .fastq, .fasta, .bed and their usual spellings, with or without a .gz.

So K03455.1 has a dot and is not a file. SRR8525904, sample_a and patient-04 have neither, and nothing is said about them.

docs.title: The assumption only the step can see
docs.text:
The other kind of note is not in the file at all, and no amount of reading one would find it.

bcftools call -mv writes only the sites it called a variant at. A position missing from a VCF is therefore ambiguous between two things with opposite clinical meanings: the sample agrees with the reference, which is a susceptible result, or nothing aligned there, which is no result at all. Resolving that towards the first manufactures susceptible calls out of dropouts, which is the thing D29 exists to refuse.

So resistance interpretation reads the alignment for coverage where it is given. Where it is not, it has to assume something, and the assumption it makes has a direction — and here is the problem the note solves. The report cannot say so. Its unread column is empty when nothing is known to be unread, which is exactly what a perfectly covered sample's report looks like. Two runs, one with full coverage and one with no coverage at all, can come out byte for byte the same.

Nothing downstream can recover the difference, so the step that knows says it, and the engine carries it (D32):

$ ligase run
ran       `resistance` (sample SRR8525904)   1.2s

noticed   `resistance` (sample SRR8525904): no alignment was supplied, so coverage is unknown, no codon can be phased, and every position the caller did not report is taken to be reference
          Pass the alignment — `coverage=aln` — so uncalled positions are reported as unread rather than as reference.

3 steps: 3 ran.

The same channel carries the hedges a reading makes with an alignment, which are the ones a real sample usually produces: a gene no codon of which reached the depth asked for, a gene only partly read, and codons no read spans all three bases of, which are read base by base and can name a mutation no single read carries (D31).

Each of those is the difference between a score and a floor, which is a clinical distinction. None of them changes a result: a note never does.

docs.title: Why a note and not a column
docs.text:
A column in the report would travel with the file, which is a real advantage, and it was not chosen for two reasons.

The report's columns are part of what a report is — the canonical hash keeps the header as a row — so adding one changes every report's hash and makes a comparison against Stanford's own reports harder to read, which is what validation rests on. And the sentence would be repeated on all twenty-seven rows, because the hedge is about the reading rather than about any one drug.

The deciding argument is that a note is not only for the person reading one report. It reaches the run report, the provenance record, the bundle and the methods section, in the same words each time, which is where a reviewer asking "what did this rest on?" will be looking.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A Ligase pipeline is a graph of steps, built from the signatures of decorated Python functions and checked before any of them runs.

@lg.step(tool="minimap2")
def align(reads: Reads, ref: Reference) -> Alignment:
    return lg.sh("minimap2 -ax sr {ref} {reads.r1} {reads.r2} | samtools sort -o {out}")

@lg.step reads that signature once, when the module is imported. Two parameters take data; one returns data. That is enough to know what align consumes and produces — and it is all Ligase ever looks at, because calling align(reads, hxb2) does not run the function. It records the call and hands back a handle on an alignment that does not exist yet.

Chain the handles, hand the last one to lg.Pipeline, and you have a graph:

pipe = lg.Pipeline(samples.map(lambda s: resistance(call(align(s, hxb2), hxb2))))
pipe.check()      # type-checks every step. Nothing runs.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
A workflow manager runs your steps and tells you afterwards. If step four was handed the wrong reference, you find out when step four finishes — or, worse, you do not find out at all, because it finished successfully and produced plausible numbers for the wrong genome.

Deferring the bodies turns that around. The graph exists before the compute does, so the question "do these steps fit together?" can be answered in milliseconds:

$ ligase check
checked 2 steps in pipeline.py

DimensionError in step `call`:
  aln.organism = HIV-1 (from step `align`)
  ref.organism = human (declared)
  These must match. Did you pass data from the wrong organism?

DimensionError in step `call`:
  aln.reference = HXB2 (from step `align`)
  ref.reference = hg38 (from FASTA contigs: refs/hg38.fasta)
  Contig `1`: same name and length but different sequence (MD5 a965a71a against 44e7acaf).
  These must match. Did you pass the wrong reference?

2 errors in 1 step.

Two mistakes, both found, before a single read was aligned.

docs.title: Dimensions travel through the graph
docs.text:
align was never run, so where did aln.organism come from?

A step's output carries the dimensions of its inputs. The reference went in, so the reference comes out; the reads' sample identity and pairing come out with it. The provenance says which step it came through:

>>> aligned = align(reads, hxb2)
>>> pipe = lg.Pipeline(call(aligned, hxb2))
>>> for name, value in lg.handle(aligned).dataset.dimensions.items():
...     print(f"{name} = {value.value} ({value.source})")
organism = HIV-1 (from step `align`)
reference = HXB2 (from step `align`)
contig_naming = bare (Ensembl/NCBI style) (from step `align`)
coordinates = 1-based closed (from step `align`)
sample_set = [reads_phred33] (from step `align`)
pairing = paired-end (from step `align`)

This is an alignment Ligase has worked out the properties of without producing it. coordinates is the one dimension it did not inherit: alignments are 1-based closed by specification and nothing upstream of one has a coordinate system at all, so the step is where the convention appears.

docs.title: Unknown until somebody asks
docs.text:
The catalogue has a rule that only a graph can enforce:

Unknown dimensions are allowed only if no downstream step requires them.

A BAM with no @RG lines does not know its sample. Feed it through one call step and nothing cares, because nothing in that pipeline joins two sample sets together:

>>> lg.Pipeline(call(aln, hxb2)).report().summary
'no problems found.'

Merge two sets of calls, though, and the sample identity suddenly matters — mixing up which column belongs to which patient is the kind of error that produces entirely plausible results. Now it is reported, against the file you have to change:

UndeclaredDimensionError in step `merge`:
  sample_set is unknown in data/sample.bam (no @RG lines with an SM tag in the header)
  It reaches `merge` through step `call`.
  `merge` needs sample_set to agree. Declare it where you load the data.

Notice what that message does. You are looking at a step called merge, but the thing to fix is a BAM two steps upstream, and the error says so and says how the one reaches the other. Reported once, however many steps the gap travels through — a single missing declaration is one thing to fix, not one error per step it passes.

docs.title: Intervals, and the dimension that was waiting for them
docs.text:
coordinates has been in the catalogue from the start and had almost nothing to do: SAM, BAM and VCF are all 1-based closed. Intervals are where it earns its place, because BED is 0-based half-open and GFF is 1-based closed, and nothing in the file tells you which a tool expected.

>>> regions = lg.intervals("data/regions.bed")
>>> pipe = lg.Pipeline(restrict(call(aligned, hxb2), regions))
>>> pipe.check()
DimensionError in step `restrict`:
  v.coordinates = 1-based closed (from step `call`)
  regions.coordinates = 0-based half-open (from BED coordinate convention: data/regions.bed)
  These must match. Did you mean to convert between coordinate systems?

No checksum would have caught that. Both files are valid, both describe the same contigs of the same reference, and every result is off by one base.

docs.title: Per-sample fan-out
docs.text:
lg.samples() globs a directory, pairs the mates and loads each sample:

samples = lg.samples("data/*.fastq.gz", paired=True)
pipe = lg.Pipeline(samples.map(lambda s: resistance(call(align(s, hxb2), hxb2))))

map applies the chain once per sample, so three samples give three chains in one graph — and one shared reference node, because it is one file. The graph is fully expanded before anything runs, which is what lets the executor schedule it; running the chains in parallel and caching each sample separately is the executor's.

Fan-out changes what a report has to say. One written call step is now one step per sample, so an error has to name which one, and a count of failing steps has to count places rather than names:

$ ligase check
checked 8 steps in pipeline.py

DimensionError in step `call` (sample SRR32217714):
  aln.reference = HXB2 (from step `align`)
  ref.reference = hg38 (from FASTA contigs: data/refs/hg38.fasta)
  Contig `K03455.1` is not in hg38.
  These must match. Did you pass the wrong reference?
  The same problem affects 3 other samples: SRR32217715, SRR32217716, SRR32217726.

4 errors in 4 steps.

Three things are going on in that output, and each of them is the difference between a report you can act on and one you cannot.

The heading names the sample, because under fan-out the node is the sample. Without it those four errors are byte-identical and you cannot tell whether you are looking at one problem or four.

It appears only when it is needed. A step whose name belongs to one step is not annotated at all — the error reads in step \call`:`, as the examples above do, because there was nothing you were struggling to identify. And where a name is shared but the samples do not differ, the sample is not what tells those steps apart, so something that does is used instead:

ContigNamingError in step `call` (file data/alignments/run_b.bam):

If nothing separates them cleanly, nothing is added. A suffix that repeats looks exactly like an identifier while being none.

The count is of steps that failed, not of step names that failed. "4 errors in 4 steps" says a cohort-wide problem; "4 errors in 1 step" — which is what a count by name gives you — says a localised one, and the two call for completely different responses.

The problem itself is stated once. On four hundred samples the alternative is four hundred identical paragraphs. Every affected sample is still named rather than counted, so you never have to expand anything to find out who was hit, and a sample whose problem differs keeps its own paragraph rather than being folded in:

ContigNamingError in step `call` (sample SRR32217726):
  aln.contig_naming = chr-prefixed (UCSC style) (from step `align`)
  ref.contig_naming = bare (Ensembl/NCBI style) (from FASTA deflines: refs/hg38.fasta)
  The contigs are otherwise identical. Add a renaming step, or use one naming style throughout.

In Python the collapsing is not applied to the list — pipe.errors() has one error per failing step, each with its own scope — so the question you actually have is one comprehension away:

>>> affected = {error.scope[1] for error in pipe.errors() if error.scope}
>>> sorted(affected)
['SRR32217714', 'SRR32217715', 'SRR32217716', 'SRR32217726']

docs.title: What is not here yet
docs.text:
The graph is built, checked and run — see running a pipeline for lg.sh, the cache and what pipe.run() reports. What a step body returns is covered there too, since a body describes work rather than doing it.

pipe.methods() and ligase methods arrive with provenance in M5: the engine records a step's tool versions and parameters today, but nothing turns them into a methods paragraph or a reproducibility bundle yet.

Conversions are still v2. check() reports that a BED and a VCF disagree about coordinates; it does not go looking for the conversion that would fix it (D5).

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Ligase is one repository holding three layers: a Rust engine, a thin binding crate, and a Python package. One pip install gets you all three.

crates/ligase-core/   Rust engine. Published as the `ligase` crate.
crates/ligase-py/     PyO3 bindings. Compiled to `ligase._core`.
python/ligase/        The Python API you import.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
The two requirements pull in opposite directions.

Scientists live in Python. An API that is not importable from a notebook will not be used, however correct it is.

But the parts of Ligase that must not be wrong — dimension checking, content hashing of multi-gigabyte BAMs, graph construction, the cache — want a language with real types and real speed. Hashing a 40 GB alignment in Python is not a serious proposal, and a type system that silently coerces is not a type system.

So the engine is Rust and the surface is Python (decision D1). The boundary between them is deliberately narrow.

docs.title: crates/ligase-core — the engine
docs.text:
The correctness-critical logic: biological types and their dimensions, the dimension checker, the dependency graph, the content-addressed cache, the executor, provenance recording.

This crate knows nothing about Python. No pyo3 dependency, no PyObject in a signature. That keeps it testable with plain cargo test, usable from other Rust programs, and honest: if a type only makes sense because of how Python calls it, it belongs one layer up.

It is published under the name ligase, even though its directory is ligase-core. The directory says what role it plays in the workspace; the crate name is what you would type in a Cargo.toml.

docs.title: crates/ligase-py — the bindings
docs.text:
A cdylib compiled to a single shared object and imported as ligase._core. Its job is translation and nothing else: take Python arguments, call the engine, turn Rust errors into Python exceptions.

It is private, by the leading underscore and by intent. It is also publish = false — it is not a Rust library anyone should depend on.

docs.title: python/ligase — the surface
docs.text:
The public API: the @lg.step decorator, lg.Pipeline, the type names, the CLI. This is what the golden example imports.

Python is the right language for this layer. Decorators that read function signatures, friendly error messages, notebook integration — all of it is easier and better in Python, and none of it is correctness-critical.

docs.title: Why the extension module is private
docs.text:
ligase._core is an implementation detail. Nothing outside python/ligase/__init__.py should import it.

This matters more than it looks. The compiled module is where the Rust/Python boundary lives, and that boundary will move: a function that starts in Python may move into Rust for speed, and a Rust function may gain a Python wrapper that does argument validation. If users import ligase._core directly, every such move is a breaking change. With the boundary hidden, it is an implementation detail.

The version is the smallest example of the pattern already in place:

>>> import ligase
>>> ligase.__version__        # Python attribute...
'0.1.0'
>>> ligase._core.version()    # ...reporting what Rust was compiled as
'0.1.0'

__version__ is not a string typed into a Python file. It is read from the compiled engine, so a wheel cannot report a version it was not built from — a small instance of the same principle the cache rests on: never trust metadata you can derive from content.

docs.title: Where everything else lives
docs.text:
tests/              pytest acceptance tests (the Python side)
scripts/            fetch_test_data.sh and friends
docs/               this site, including the design docs
data/               fetched test data. Gitignored, never committed.

Test data is downloaded, not committed, and pinned by checksum. See installation.
