docs.title: How was this produced?
docs.text:
A cache answers one question: has this been computed? It is designed to be thrown away, because everything in it can be computed again.

This is a different question, and the answer to it cannot be recomputed. The machine that produced a result a year ago, the version of the aligner that was installed that week, the exact command that ran — none of those come back. If they were not written down at the time, they are gone.

docs.title: The hole semantic hashing left
docs.text:
Ligase hashes an output by what it means rather than by the bytes it holds, and it has to: every real tool writes its own command line into the file it produces, that command line contains the output path, and the output path is a staging file named after the step's own key. So before M4 a step's output bytes contained that step's own key, and any change to a step at all — a comment — cascaded to the bottom of the pipeline.

Dropping those fields fixed that and cost something real (D22):

a cache hit can no longer prove which command produced an object, because the field that said so is not in the hash.

That field was the only thing in the system that said how an object was made. So provenance is not an extra feature bolted on beside the cache — it is the thing that makes dropping @PG affordable.

docs.title: What is recorded, and when
docs.text:
A step that runs writes down how it ran: the command with its placeholders filled in, every tool and the whole of what --version printed, every parameter as it was hashed, every input by content hash, and every reference by accession and checksum. A step served from the cache writes nothing and needs to — the record from the run that did the work is still there.

That is why ligase methods on a pipeline that recomputed nothing still names every command:

$ ligase run
cached    `align` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942
cached    `call` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942
cached    `resistance` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942

12 steps: 12 from cache.

$ ligase methods
`align` ran on 4 samples (SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942)
with minimap2 2.31-r1302 and samtools 1.24, as `minimap2 -t {threads} -ax sr
{ref} {reads.r1} {reads.r2} | samtools sort -@ {threads} -o {out}`, with
threads = 4, against the HXB2 reference (K03455.1, 9719 bp, MD5
c66838498aab02f786a6ec2f2d62cdc1).

docs.title: It outlives the cache
docs.text:
The cache throws away its tables whenever the key format changes, because an entry composed under different rules is not stale — it is a claim about ingredients that were combined differently, and reading it would be worse than recomputing. None of that reasoning touches a record of what a command did. That stays true however the engine later decides to compose keys.

So provenance is a separate database with a separate lifetime (D23): provenance.sqlite beside cache.sqlite. Delete the cache to its foundations and the answer to "how was this produced?" survives.

docs.title: A reference needs nothing new to be pinned
docs.text:
CLAUDE.md asks for remote data to be pinned by accession, version and checksum. For a reference FASTA, all three were already being read.

HXB2's defline is:

>K03455.1 Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HXB2), complete genome; ...

The loader already takes the first token as the sequence name — so the accession with its version is right there — and already computes the MD5 of the sequence, uppercased with whitespace removed, because that is the digest the SAM specification defines for @SQ M5. Nothing is declared and nothing is invented.

A name is only called an accession when it looks like one. chr1 is a sequence name, and a methods section that cited it as an accession would be worse than one that admitted it had none — so a reference with no accession to give is pinned by its fingerprint instead, which is always there.

docs.title: What a gap is
docs.text:
A step whose output sits in the cache from before provenance was kept has no record, and nothing can reconstruct one. ligase methods says so, by name:

`align` (4 samples) is in the cache from a run that recorded no provenance,
so how it was produced is not known here. `ligase run --force` runs it again
and records it.

That is the same instinct as the dimension checker reporting a dimension as unknown rather than guessing it. A paragraph that silently omitted a step would be exactly the failure this milestone exists to prevent.

docs.title: The bundle, and what it can honestly claim
docs.text:
ligase methods --bundle DIR writes everything another machine needs in order to check the results — and not the data, which for the reference pipeline is gigabytes of sequencing reads (D25). The data is named instead: every input by content hash, every reference by accession and checksum. Nothing else will satisfy the check.

What the bundle claims is testable: a run elsewhere lands on the same canonical hashes. ligase methods --verify DIR is that check, and the interesting one of its four answers is the second:

Verdict What it means identical The same key and the same result. Nothing feeding the step moved. reproduced A different key and the same result anyway — a tool version or a platform moved and the science did not. differs A different result. A finding. missing The bundle expected a step this pipeline no longer produces.

reproduced is what a reviewer on another machine actually gets, and being able to report it is the reason a bundle is worth writing.

Inputs are checked by content too, which is not a bonus: without it a differs would be uninterpretable, because a changed input explains a changed output.

docs.title: Resistance interpretation
docs.text:
Every other part of Ligase is about keeping data straight. This is the one part that says what the data means: it takes variant calls against HXB2, works out which amino acids each codon of protease, reverse transcriptase, integrase and capsid holds, and scores them against the Stanford HIVdb algorithm.

@lg.step(tool="hivdb")
def resistance(
    v: Variants, ref: Reference, aln: Alignment
) -> ResistanceReport:
    return lg.hivdb.interpret(v, ref, coverage=aln)

The output is one row per drug: a score, a level from Susceptible to High-Level Resistance, the mutations that got it there, and the algorithm that decided.

docs.title: The rules are vendored, not fetched
docs.text:
Stanford publishes the HIVdb algorithm as ASI2 XML in its own repository, hivdb/hivfacts, under the Unlicense — a dedication to the public domain. Ligase ships two versions of it, pinned by checksum: 9.8, which is what the published results it is validated against were produced with, and 10.2, which is current.

Stanford also runs a web service that does this interpretation. Ligase does not call it, and the reason is the same one behind every other decision here: an answer that depends on the day it was asked for is not reproducible. No cache key can see a remote service change its mind, and no reproducibility bundle can carry it. docs/decisions.md D8 puts public-data fetching out of scope for v0.1 in any case.

So the rules are part of the engine, and which rules were used is part of the cache key — by the digest of their bytes rather than by their version number. Upstream publishes corrections under near-identical names (HIVDB_10.0 and HIVDB_10.0-1 both exist), and a key that moved only with the name would happily serve a result computed under rules that have since changed.

docs.title: Four judgements, all made the same way
docs.text: An interpretation can be wrong in two directions, and they are not equally bad. Reporting resistance that is not there costs a patient a drug they could have taken. Reporting susceptibility that is not there costs them a drug that will fail. Everywhere these two could be traded off, Ligase takes the first.

docs.title: A mixture is every amino acid it could be
docs.text:
Where the reads support both the reference base and an alternate above the mixture threshold, the codon holds both amino acids, and a rule is satisfied if any of them satisfies it.

An ambiguous position is two viruses, not an average of one. Taking the majority base would discard the minority virus — which is the entire reason anyone sequences deeply, and which in practice is where resistance shows up first.

docs.title: A codon is only the combinations the reads carry
docs.text:
A mixture at two bases of one codon is where the first judgement could go wrong on its own. A VCF says what is at each position, not what travels together, so enumerating the combinations of two ambiguous bases invents codons no read carries.

On Sample 3 of PRJNA1218827 the caller credits G at the first base of RT codon 219 in 43% of the reads there and at the second base in 2.4%. At a 2% threshold both pass, and the four combinations spell lysine, arginine, glutamate and glycine — where the reads spanning the whole codon carry two of them: AAA in 54% of themselves and GAA in 45%. The other two are under two tenths of a per cent each.

So the alignment settles it. Reads spanning all three bases are counted as the triplets they carry, and the codon holds the amino acids whose share of those reads reaches the mixture threshold. Two rules keep this from going wrong in the other direction:

  • Phasing narrows a reading and never widens one. What is present at a position stays the caller's judgement, which weighs base quality; the reads only decide which combinations of called alleles are real.
  • A codon no read spans keeps its per-base reading, noted rather than dropped or guessed at — see D31, which also says how far that note is visible today.

docs.title: A position that was not read is not a wild-type position
docs.text:
bcftools writes only the sites it has something to say about. A position missing from a VCF is therefore ambiguous between "agrees with the reference" and "nothing aligned here" — and those have opposite clinical meanings.

So coverage is read from the alignment. A codon whose bases are not all covered to the required depth is unread, not reference, and a drug whose rules mention an unread position reports its score as a floor rather than as an answer, naming the positions it could not see.

Without an alignment nothing can be known about coverage, and the reading says so in a note rather than assuming quietly. That assumption has a direction — it manufactures susceptible results out of dropouts — and the one thing it must never be is silent. The report itself cannot say it, since a report with nothing known to be unread looks exactly like one that was fully covered, so the step hands the note to the engine and the engine says it: in the run report, in provenance, in a bundle and in the methods section (D32).

The hedges a reading makes with an alignment travel the same way. A gene no codon of which reached the depth asked for, a gene only partly read, and codons no read spans all three bases of are each the difference between a score and a floor, and each is said rather than left for someone to infer from an unread column.

The test that pins this is a no-template control. Sixty of its thirty-two thousand reads map to HXB2. A pipeline that read "no variant called" as "agrees with the reference" would report a tube of water as fully susceptible to all twenty-seven drugs.

docs.title: A gene nobody sequenced is not assessed
docs.text:
HIVDB 9.8 scores lenacapavir against capsid, which is in gag. A pipeline that sequenced only pol has nothing whatever to say about it — so the report says "Not assessed" rather than "Susceptible".

This is D24's reasoning about citations applied to a drug class: a gap that is named is honest, and a gap that is filled with a cheerful default is not.

docs.title: What it is checked against
docs.text:
The scoring engine reproduces 3,348 published Stanford HIVdb results exactly — thirty clinical samples at four ambiguity thresholds, every drug, every score, every level. Those expectations come from Sierra 3.5.3, a different implementation in a different language by the algorithm's own authors, so agreeing with them is evidence rather than circularity.

The pipeline end to end is checked in validation.

docs.title: What a file means, and what bytes it holds
docs.text:
A step reruns when something that could change its result has changed. The question "has it changed?" is answered by hashing, and hashing has to be asked about the right thing.

Bytes are the obvious answer and the wrong one. Here is why, in the words of the tools themselves.

docs.title: Every real tool signs its work
docs.text:
Run minimap2 and look at the header of the BAM it wrote:

@PG  ID:minimap2  PN:minimap2  VN:2.31-r1302  CL:minimap2 -t 8 -ax sr refs/HXB2.fasta SRR8525904_1.fastq.gz SRR8525904_2.fastq.gz

bcftools does the same, with the time of day beside it:

##bcftools_callCommand=call -mv --ploidy 1 -Oz -o /tmp/out.vcf.gz; Date=Sat Oct 17 21:14:12 2026

Neither line is a result. Both are in the file, so both are in its bytes — and a cache that compares bytes thinks two runs that computed exactly the same alignments produced different things.

It is worse than untidy. Look at what is inside that CL: — the output path. Ligase writes a step's output into a staging file named after the step's own key, so the bytes of a step's output contain the step's own key. Change anything about align at all, even a comment, and its bytes move; the step below is keyed on those bytes, so it reruns, and its bytes move too. The rerun reaches the bottom of the pipeline however identical the science. Early cutoff could not survive contact with a real aligner.

docs.title: So a file is hashed by what it means
docs.text:
Before an output is hashed it is canonicalised: its records are sorted, and the fields that record when and how it was made rather than what is in it are dropped (D4). What is hashed is what is left.

$ ligase run                       # after `threads=1`
$ ligase run                       # with threads=8
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525904)   3.3s
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525908)   6.9s
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525920)   3.7s
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525942)   6.0s
skipped   `call` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942
skipped   `resistance` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942

12 steps: 4 ran, 8 skipped.

align reran, and it had to: a thread count is a parameter of the step, and nothing can know in advance that -t 8 will not change an answer. What the engine can know, once the step has rerun, is whether the answer changed — and it did not, so the eight steps below it had nothing to do.

docs.title: The canonical form belongs to the type, not to the step
docs.text:
A BAM, a VCF and a FASTA each have their own notion of what they say and their own volatile fields, so each has its own canonical form. Which one applies comes from the type the data carries, not from the step that produced it — so two steps writing alignments are compared the same way, and the rules for a format live in one place.

Type Dropped as volatile Records Reads the description after a read's name sorted Reference descriptions, line wrapping, case in order Alignment @PG, @HD, @CO sorted Variants dates, sources, ##reference paths, tool command lines sorted Intervals track, browser and comment lines sorted ResistanceReport — header kept, rows sorted

docs.title: Why some formats sort and others do not
docs.text:
Because that question was already answered, by D14, for the dimension checker: a sequence dictionary's contig order is semantic, since GATK requires two of them to agree on it, while a BED's record order is whatever order the intervals happened to be sorted in.

So a reference's contigs and a BAM's @SQ lines keep their order, and alignment records, variant records, intervals, reads and report rows are sorted. The same line, drawn once, in two places.

docs.title: A tolerance, where a number cannot be expected to repeat
docs.text:
QUAL in a VCF is a Phred-scaled floating-point accumulation, and the order the terms were added in can move its last digits. A variant called at 215.376 on one machine and 215.375 on another is the same finding.

So a numeric field may declare a tolerance, and QUAL declares one of a tenth of a Phred unit — two orders of magnitude below the smallest threshold anyone filters on, so it cannot merge two qualities a user would treat differently. Everything else is exact: a tolerance nobody has measured would be a guess baked into every cache key, and a cache that is too cold costs time while one that is too warm is wrong.

A tolerance is expressed by quantising — putting the value in a bucket of that width and hashing the bucket — and that has a consequence worth knowing (D20): two values closer together than the tolerance can still fall either side of a bucket edge.

docs.title: When the file is not what its name says
docs.text:
Canonicalising means parsing, and parsing can fail: a truncated BAM, a .vcf.gz that is not gzipped, a file still being written. Such a file falls back to the hash of its bytes, tagged as such (D21). Bytes are the stricter test, so the fallback can cost a rerun but can never serve a wrong answer.

Every parser is strict for the same reason: one that read what it could and ignored the rest would let two files that differ in the skipped part agree, which is the one failure a cache must never have.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
One pass over each file, once. What a file means is remembered against the hash of its bytes, so a file is parsed the first time it is seen and never again — not on the next run, not after it is copied, not when another step produces it identically:

$ ligase run                       # nothing has changed
12 steps: 12 from cache.

No file was read and none was parsed. The prefilter still does the first part of that job, and the canonical hashes sit behind it.

docs.title: Asking the question directly
docs.text:
Semantic hashing answers "did this change?" by not running things. The opposite question — "would this come out the same if I ran it again?" — needs something that does:

$ ligase audit align --sample SRR8525904
reproducible     `align` (sample SRR8525904)
    the bytes differ            36696dacb83d / a96bfeff4e26
    what they mean does not     43c4c32bbd53

1 step: 1 reproducible.

See auditing a step for what the three verdicts mean and when to reach for them.

docs.title: What this is
docs.text:
A Ligase dataset is not just a file path. It is a kind of biological data — reads, a reference, an alignment, variant calls — carrying the dimensions of what is inside it: which organism, which reference build, which coordinate convention, which samples in which order.

import ligase as lg

hxb2 = lg.reference("data/refs/HXB2.fasta", organism="HIV-1", build="HXB2")
aln = lg.alignment("data/alignments/SRR32217714.bam")

lg.check_step("call", {"aln": aln, "ref": hxb2})  # nothing computed

check_step compares the dimensions and raises if they disagree. No compute runs, no files are written, and the whole thing takes milliseconds.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
The worst computational biology bugs are silent. Aligning to hg19 and annotating against hg38. Feeding 0-based half-open intervals to a tool that expects 1-based closed. chr1 against 1. A sample column that shifted by one somewhere in a join. None of these crash. All of them produce plausible numbers that are wrong, and the wrongness can survive peer review.

Workflow managers move files between steps extremely well, but a file path is an opaque token to them: they cannot tell you that the BAM in slot one and the FASTA in slot two describe different genomes. Ligase reads the headers, learns what the dimensions are, and refuses the connection.

The physics analogy is exact. You would not add metres to seconds. A reference build is a unit, and so is a coordinate convention.

docs.title: The dimensions
docs.text:
The full catalogue, including which formats can state which dimension, is in Dimensions. In brief:

Dimension What it captures organism HIV-1, SARS-CoV-2, human reference The build, by contig identity — not by name contig_naming chr1 against 1 coordinates 0-based half-open against 1-based closed sample_set The sample identifiers, in order pairing Single-end against paired-end quality_encoding Phred+33 against Phred+64

Each dimension is inferred from the file where the format records it, and declared by the user once where it does not. A FASTA cannot tell you its organism; a BAM @SQ header can tell you its reference exactly.

docs.title: Three ideas that make this work
Reference identity is contigs, never filenames
docs.text:
A reference's identity is its contig names, their lengths, and their MD5 checksums where available. Not the filename, and not a label you gave it.

This matters because filenames lie constantly. genome.fa on two machines is two different genomes. A directory called hg38 can hold hg19. Worse, a label can be right and still useless: hg19 and hg38 both have a chr1, and distinguishing them needs the sequence itself.

So Ligase computes each contig's MD5 from the FASTA, reads the @SQ M5 an aligner wrote into a BAM, and compares them. If an aligner claims your BAM is on a reference whose chr1 has a different checksum from the chr1 in the FASTA you just passed, that is caught before anything runs.

A label such as HXB2 is kept, but only to make error messages readable. When two references describe themselves identically — two files both labelled hg38 — the message falls back to showing their fingerprints, because a message that prints the same value twice cannot be acted on.

docs.title: Provenance travels inside the value
docs.text:
Every dimension value carries where it came from. Not reconstructed when an error is built; stored alongside the value from the moment it is read.

That is the difference between an error you can act on and one that sends you hunting:

DimensionError in step `call`:
  aln.reference = HXB2 (from BAM @SQ header: data/sample.bam)
  ref.reference = hg38 (from FASTA contigs: refs/hg38.fasta)
  These must match. Did you pass the wrong reference?

You know which two files to look at and which part of each one said what.

docs.title: Unknown is a real answer
docs.text:
Where a format cannot state a dimension, Ligase says so and says why, rather than guessing:

>>> ref = lg.reference("data/refs/HXB2.fasta")
>>> ref.dimension("organism") is None
True
>>> ref.unknown_reason("organism")
'a FASTA does not record its organism; declare it'

A guess that happens to be wrong passes check() silently, which is the exact failure mode this project exists to remove. So a FASTQ whose quality scores fall in the range Phred+33 and Phred+64 share reports its encoding as unknown; guessing would shift every quality value by 31 and nothing downstream would notice.

"Unknown" is distinct from "does not apply". A reference has no quality encoding at all — that is a category error, not a gap — and check_step never asks you to fill it in.

docs.title: When a dimension must be known
docs.text:
Ligase draws a line between two things:

  • Checked — whenever two inputs both state a value, those values must agree. Always, for every dimension. This costs nothing and demands nothing.
  • Required — additionally, the value must not be unknown. Only where a disagreement would silently corrupt results.

Checking an alignment against a reference requires the reference dimension: an alignment that cannot say what it was aligned to is not something to shrug at. But aligning reads to a reference requires nothing, because introducing the reference is what alignment does.

This line is deliberate, and it errs toward demanding less. A checker that cries wolf gets bypassed, and a bypassed checker catches nothing. Correct input that gets rejected is not a safe failure — it is how users learn to stop trusting the tool.

docs.title: Coordinates, and the type that needed them
docs.text:
coordinates sat in the catalogue doing almost nothing for a milestone, because SAM, BAM and VCF are all 1-based closed and a lossless re-encoding between containers changes nothing (D9).

Intervals is what it was waiting for. BED is 0-based half-open and GFF is 1-based closed, and feeding one to a tool that expected the other produces results that are off by exactly one base and look entirely plausible:

>>> regions = lg.intervals("data/regions.bed")
>>> regions.dimension("coordinates").value
'0-based half-open'

An interval file's contigs come from its records, so they carry no length and no checksum — a BED records neither, and inventing them would be the lie this whole system guards against. They are still compared against a reference by name, which is enough to catch a chr-prefixed BED against a bare reference, or an interval on a contig the reference does not have.

Their order, on the other hand, is not compared at all. The contigs of a sequence dictionary have a meaningful order — GATK requires two dictionaries to agree on it — but the contigs of a BED's records appear in whatever order the intervals were sorted in. Reporting that as a contig order mismatch would be a false alarm, and false alarms are how a correctness tool gets switched off.

docs.title: What is not here yet
docs.text: Dimensions are checked where steps meet. They are not converted: a typed liftover that the engine could search for to fix a mismatch automatically is v2, and the design note is D5.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
docs/milestones.md signs M6 off when "resistance calls match published results ... with discrepancies explained". This is what was compared, what agreed, and what did not.

Everything here is reproduced by tests/test_validation.py, which runs the real pipeline over real reads on every CI run of the demo job.

docs.title: Two things are validated, separately
docs.text:
The scoring engine is checked against Stanford's own answers. crates/ligase-core/tests/fixtures/hivdb/ holds the Stanford HIVdb reports published as supplementary data by the HIVGenoPipe study — thirty clinical samples at four ambiguity thresholds, 3,348 expectations — produced by Sierra 3.5.3 against HIVDB 9.8.

All 3,348 are reproduced exactly: every drug, every score, every level.

That oracle matters because the obvious alternative is circular. Checking the scorer against expectations derived from the same XML it reads would test the parser against itself. Sierra is a different implementation, in a different language, by the algorithm's own authors.

The pipeline end to end is checked by running it on reads whose published answers are known, which is the rest of this page.

docs.title: The samples
docs.text:
PRJNA1218827 is the HIVGenoPipe study's MiSeq data. Four runs are fetched, and the SRA metadata maps each to the sample identifier the paper uses — so nothing rests on reading a figure.

Run Sample What it is SRR32217726 Sample 3 a mixture: K219KE, and L100LI below it SRR32217715 Sample 4 multi-class positive: NRTI, INSTI and capsid SRR32217716 Sample 30 fully susceptible — a clean negative SRR32217714 — the study's no-template control

A mixture, a strong positive, a true negative and a blank. Between them they exercise every judgement the interpreter makes.

docs.title: What agrees
docs.text:
The pipeline's mixture parameter answers the same question as the paper's Amb2/Amb5/Amb15 reports, so one set of alignments validates all three thresholds.

Threshold Drug calls compared Agree 15% 81 81 5% 81 81 2% 81 72

At 15% and 5% the agreement is exact — every score, every level, every mutation string, for all twenty-seven drugs on all three samples.

That includes the cases worth naming:

  • Sample 3 at 15%: K219KE, potential low-level resistance to zidovudine and stavudine. A mixture, scored as both amino acids.
  • Sample 3 at 5%: adds L100LI — high-level resistance to four NNRTIs. Same reads, same alignment; a 5% minority virus changes the regimen.
  • Sample 4: M184V, T97A + E138T + G140S + Q148H giving high-level resistance to all five INSTIs, and M66I + Q67H + N74D + A105T in capsid giving high-level lenacapavir resistance at a score of 160.
  • Sample 30: susceptible on all twenty-seven, with no false positives.
  • The no-template control: all twenty-seven drugs Not assessed, with no score. Sixty of its thirty-two thousand reads map to HXB2.

docs.title: What disagrees, and why
docs.text:
Three of the 243 drug calls differ, all of them at the 2% threshold, and all three are the same missed mutation counted once per drug. They are listed with their cause in KNOWN_AT_TWO_PERCENT in tests/test_validation.py, and the test fails if one of them changes shape or a new one appears — which is what keeps "discrepancies explained" from decaying into "discrepancies tolerated".

It was nine until codons were read from the reads rather than from the combinations of their bases. Six were a phasing artefact, and what fixed them is below.

docs.title: Three are one missed mutation, and it is a real one
docs.text:
Stanford reports V75VA for Sample 30 at 2%, reading potential low-level resistance to zidovudine, intermediate to stavudine and low-level to didanosine. Ligase reports susceptible to all three.

The caller credits the V75A base in 4 of the 239 reads it counted at HXB2 2773 — 1.7%, below the threshold that would report it. HIVGenoPipe realigns against a sample-specific reference, which is that paper's whole method, and places reads that an alignment to HXB2 does not.

This is a sensitivity limit, not a disagreement about what the reads mean, and it is the honest cost of the demo's approach. It is also the only disagreement left that would change what anyone did.

Phasing does not reach it, and must not. The raw read bases at 2773 carry the alanine base in 3.2% of themselves, where bcftools mpileup credits 1.7% once base quality is taken into account. Counting raw bases would "find" V75A at a 2% threshold and would agree with the published report by accident, on evidence the caller had already judged too poor to report. Which alleles are present stays the caller's judgement; phasing only decides which combinations of called alleles are real (D31).

docs.title: What this exercise changed about the pipeline
docs.text: Validating is what found the biggest problem, and it was not in the interpreter. It also found the second, which was.

docs.title: Codons are read from the reads, not from the combinations
docs.text:
Sample 3's five NRTI rows used to read K219KEGR where Stanford reads K219KE, and Sample 4's lenacapavir row A105AT where Stanford reads A105T: six discrepancies, every score and level identical, only the mutation string wrong.

A codon was assembled from the VCF — the alleles credited at each of the three bases, then every combination of them. The caller credits G at HXB2 3204 in 43% of the reads it counted and at 3205 in 2.4%, so at a 2% threshold both pass and the combinations give AAA, AGA, GAA, GGA — K, R, E and G. Of the 4,347 reads spanning the whole codon, 54% carry AAA and 45% carry GAA; AGA and GGA are under two tenths of a per cent each. Fewer than two reads in a thousand carried both substitutions. A VCF says what is at each position, not what travels together.

So codons are now read from the alignment, which was already an input for coverage: reads spanning all three bases are counted as the triplets they carry, and the codon holds the amino acids whose share of those reads reaches the threshold. Six of the nine discrepancies went with it, and the agreement at 15% and 5% is unchanged, because a majority allele is carried by the reads that support it.

docs.title: A consensus caller could not see the minority virus (M6)
docs.text:
The demo's call step used to run bcftools call -mv --ploidy 1. On Sample 3, the reads at HXB2 3204 are A 238, G 192 — a 45% K219E — and bcftools call emitted no record for it at all. The majority allele is the reference, so there was no variant to call. The report came back susceptible to all twenty-seven drugs.

It was right to, given that input: it matches Stanford's own majority-consensus report for the same sample exactly, which is itself useful evidence that the interpreter is sound. But Stanford's 5% report for that sample finds L100I as well and reads high-level resistance to four NNRTIs. A pipeline whose answer flips from "fully susceptible" to "resistant to most of the NNRTI class" on a threshold it never exposed is not doing what it says it does.

So the caller is gone, the pileup's own allele depths are the evidence, and min_freq now means what its name says.

docs.title: PRJNA517147 is not used for this
docs.text:
docs/milestones.md also names PRJNA517147, the Washington DC cohort study (Jair et al., PLoS ONE 2019;14(4):e0214820). Its per-sample resistance calls are published only as colour in a heatmap — Fig 4, reverse transcriptase only, with protease and integrase "not shown" and no supporting tables.

Of the four runs fetched from it, three are blank rows in that figure and the fourth cannot be separated from its neighbour by eye. The mutations the paper quantifies in text are attached to PL- identifiers that are never mapped to the specimen numbers the figure uses.

That project remains the demo's default dataset, and M3, M4 and M5 are still signed off on it. It is not used as a source of expected resistance answers, because a number transcribed from a figure is not a citable value. PRJNA1218827 publishes machine-readable per-sample reports with the algorithm version stamped in every row, and that is what M6 is checked against.

docs.title: Building a pipeline
docs.text: Everything here runs today. Nothing in it executes a step: the whole point is to be told your pipeline is wrong before you wait for it.

docs.title: Write a step
docs.text:
A step is an annotated function with @lg.step on it:

import ligase as lg
from ligase.types import Alignment, Reads, Reference, Variants


@lg.step(tool="minimap2")
def align(reads: Reads, ref: Reference) -> Alignment:
    return lg.sh("minimap2 -ax sr {ref} {reads.r1} {reads.r2} | samtools sort -o {out}")


@lg.step(tool="bcftools")
def call(aln: Alignment, ref: Reference, min_freq: float = 0.01) -> Variants:
    return lg.sh("bcftools mpileup -f {ref} {aln} | bcftools call -mv -Oz -o {out}")

The annotations are not documentation. They are the only description of the step that Ligase ever reads, because it never runs the body while building a graph:

  • a parameter annotated with a Ligase data type becomes a connection in the graph
  • anything else (min_freq: float = 0.01) is a plain parameter, which joins the cache key, so changing it reruns exactly the steps it could have changed
  • the return annotation is what says the step produces an Alignment

tool= names the external program the step shells out to — or several of them, tool=("minimap2", "samtools"), for a body that pipes one into the other. Each one's version belongs in the cache key, so upgrading minimap2 reruns the alignments it produced. See running a pipeline.

Leave an annotation off and you are told immediately, as the module is imported:

>>> @lg.step
... def align(reads: Reads, ref) -> Alignment: ...
StepDefinitionError: step `align` does not annotate `ref`. An unannotated
parameter might be data, and data the graph does not know about is an
unchecked connection

docs.title: Connect them
docs.text:
Calling a step records the call and returns a handle. Nothing runs:

hxb2 = lg.reference("data/refs/HXB2.fasta", organism="HIV-1", build="HXB2")
reads = lg.reads("data/runs/SRR32217714_1.fastq.gz", "data/runs/SRR32217714_2.fastq.gz")

pipe = lg.Pipeline(call(align(reads, hxb2), hxb2))
pipe.check()        # raises on the first problem; nothing is computed

lg.Pipeline walks back from the output through the handles, so the graph is built from the outputs you ask for. A file passed to two steps is one node, because it is one file:

>>> pipe = lg.Pipeline(call(align(reads, hxb2), hxb2))
>>> pipe.steps
('align', 'call')
>>> len(pipe)       # two inputs, two steps -- not three inputs
4

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
check() raises the first problem and attaches the rest. errors() returns them without raising, which is usually what you want in a notebook:

>>> for error in pipe.errors():
...     print(error)
...     print()
DimensionError in step `call`:
  aln.reference = HXB2 (from step `align`)
  ref.reference = hg38 (from FASTA contigs: data/refs/hg38.fasta)
  Contig `1`: same name and length but different sequence (MD5 a965a71a against 44e7acaf).
  These must match. Did you pass the wrong reference?

One call step, so the heading is just the step. Once you fan out, one written step is many steps and the heading says which — see many samples below.

aln.reference came out of a step that has not run. The dimensions of a step's output are worked out from its inputs, so a mistake made at the top of a pipeline is reported wherever it first matters, with the step it travelled through named.

Every error carries the whole list, so catching one shows you all of them:

>>> try:
...     pipe.check()
... except lg.CheckError as caught:
...     print(len(caught.errors), "problems")
2 problems
Catch To get lg.CheckError everything lg.DimensionError data that disagrees lg.ContigNamingError chr1 against 1 — add a renaming step lg.ContigOrderError contigs in a different dictionary order lg.UndeclaredDimensionError something to declare where you load data lg.StepTypeError a step wired to the wrong kind of data

docs.title: Many samples
docs.text:
lg.samples() globs, groups mates into samples and loads each one. .map() applies a chain to every sample:

samples = lg.samples("data/runs/*.fastq.gz", paired=True)
pipe = lg.Pipeline(samples.map(lambda s: call(align(s, hxb2), hxb2)))

>>> samples.ids
('SRR32217714', 'SRR32217715', 'SRR32217716')
>>> len(pipe)       # 3 samples + 1 reference + 3 aligns + 3 calls
10

When every sample fails the same way, the report says so once and names them all:

$ ligase check
checked 6 steps in pipeline.py

DimensionError in step `call` (sample SRR32217714):
  aln.reference = HXB2 (from step `align`)
  ref.reference = hg38 (from FASTA contigs: data/refs/hg38.fasta)
  Contig `K03455.1` is not in hg38.
  These must match. Did you pass the wrong reference?
  The same problem affects 2 other samples: SRR32217715, SRR32217716.

3 errors in 3 steps.

pipe.errors() is not collapsed — one error per failing step, each with its own sample in error.scope, which is the heading in a form you can compute with:

>>> error.scope
('sample', 'SRR32217714')
>>> sorted({e.scope[1] for e in pipe.errors() if e.scope})
['SRR32217714', 'SRR32217715', 'SRR32217716']

pipe.report().text is the collapsed form the command line prints, if you want to show it somewhere yourself.

scope is None whenever the step's own name already identifies it, which is every step in a pipeline without fan-out. Where a name is shared, the discriminator is whatever actually separates those steps — ('sample', ...) under fan-out, ('file', ...) for same-named steps over different data from one sample — and None if nothing does, because a suffix that repeats would look like an identifier without being one.

Mates are paired by filename — <sample>_1/<sample>_2 or <sample>_R1/<sample>_R2, with anything after the marker dropped, so Illumina's SAMPLE_R1_001.fastq.gz works. A file whose mate cannot be identified is an error rather than a guess:

>>> lg.samples("data/runs/*.fastq.gz", paired=True)
LoadError: cannot group reads into samples: sample `SRR32217714` has only one
of its two mates (data/runs/SRR32217714_1.fastq.gz); pass paired=False for
single-end reads

That is deliberately unhelpful about carrying on. Pairing two samples' files by accident produces results for a mixture of two people and nothing crashes.

docs.title: Intervals
docs.text:
A BED or GFF loads like anything else, and brings the coordinates dimension with it:

>>> regions = lg.intervals("data/regions.bed")
>>> regions.dimension("coordinates").value
'0-based half-open'
>>> [c.name for c in regions.contigs]
['K03455.1']

The contigs come from the records, so they have no length and no checksum — a BED records neither. They are still compared against a reference by name, which catches a chr-prefixed BED against a bare reference, and an interval on a contig the reference does not have.

Feed those intervals to a step that also takes 1-based data and you get the error the dimension exists for:

DimensionError in step `restrict`:
  v.coordinates = 1-based closed (from step `call`)
  regions.coordinates = 0-based half-open (from BED coordinate convention: data/regions.bed)
  These must match. Did you mean to convert between coordinate systems?

If a step of yours writes intervals, say which convention it writes. Alignments and variant calls are 1-based closed by specification, but a tool that writes BED from a VCF changes the convention, and inheriting the input's would be a silent lie:

@lg.step(tool="bedtools", coordinates="0-based half-open")
def windows(v: Variants) -> Intervals:
    return lg.sh("bedtools makewindows ...")

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
Put the pipeline in a file and let the CLI check it:

# pipeline.py
import ligase as lg
from ligase.types import Alignment, Reads, Reference, Variants

@lg.step(tool="minimap2")
def align(reads: Reads, ref: Reference) -> Alignment:
    return lg.sh("minimap2 -ax sr {ref} {reads.r1} {reads.r2} | samtools sort -o {out}")

@lg.step(tool="bcftools")
def call(aln: Alignment, ref: Reference, min_freq: float = 0.01) -> Variants:
    return lg.sh("bcftools mpileup -f {ref} {aln} | bcftools call -mv -Oz -o {out}")

hxb2 = lg.reference("data/refs/HXB2.fasta", organism="HIV-1", build="HXB2")
samples = lg.samples("data/runs/*.fastq.gz", paired=True)

pipe = lg.Pipeline(samples.map(lambda s: call(align(s, hxb2), hxb2)))

ligase check

$ ligase check
checked 2 steps in pipeline.py

no problems found.

With no argument it reads pipeline.py in the working directory; pass a path for anything else. The file is imported — that is how a Python pipeline declares itself — so the lg.Pipeline has to be assigned at the top level where the CLI can find it. The step bodies are still not run.

Exit codes separate the two failures worth separating:

Code Meaning 0 every pipeline in the file checks clean 1 a pipeline has errors 2 the file could not be checked at all

That makes it a CI gate:

- run: ligase check

docs.title: Declaring and checking dimensions
docs.text: A runnable walkthrough. Every snippet below works against the project's own test data.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
scripts/fetch_test_data.sh --project PRJNA1218827
scripts/make_demo_alignment.sh

The first fetches HXB2 (NCBI K03455.1) and four HIV-1 runs into a gitignored data/. The second aligns one run against HXB2 with minimap2 and writes data/alignments/<run>.bam. Both are idempotent.

docs.title: Loading data
docs.text:
import ligase as lg

hxb2 = lg.reference("data/refs/HXB2.fasta", organism="HIV-1", build="HXB2")
aln = lg.alignment("data/alignments/SRR32217714.bam")

organism and build are declared: a FASTA records neither. Everything else is read out of the files.

There are four loaders:

Loader Reads Returns lg.reference(path, ...) FASTA (optionally gzipped) Reference lg.alignment(path, ...) SAM or BAM Alignment lg.variants(path, ...) VCF (optionally gzipped or BGZF) Variants lg.reads(r1, r2, ...) FASTQ (optionally gzipped) Reads

docs.title: Inspecting what was inferred
docs.text:
>>> aln.contigs
[Contig(name='K03455.1', length=9719, md5='c66838498aab02f786a6ec2f2d62cdc1')]
>>> aln.samples
['SRR32217714']
>>> aln.dimension("reference")
DimensionValue(name='reference', value='K03455.1 (9719 bp)',
               source='from BAM @SQ header: data/alignments/SRR32217714.bam')

The source is the useful part. It tells you what to go and look at if the value is not what you expected.

Everything that has a known value:

>>> sorted(aln.dimensions)
['contig_naming', 'coordinates', 'reference', 'sample_set']

Everything that could have one for this kind of data:

>>> aln.applicable
('organism', 'reference', 'contig_naming', 'coordinates', 'sample_set', 'pairing')

organism and pairing are in the second list but not the first, so they apply but are not known. Ask why:

>>> aln.unknown_reason("organism")
'not recorded in SAM/BAM headers; declare it'

A dimension that does not apply at all returns None — there is nothing to declare:

>>> hxb2.unknown_reason("quality_encoding") is None
True

docs.title: Checking a step
docs.text:
>>> lg.check_step("call", {"aln": aln, "ref": hxb2})

Silence means the dimensions agree. Nothing was computed; the check reads headers only.

The keys are the names the step knows its inputs by, and they appear in the error messages, so name them the way your step function does.

docs.title: A different reference
docs.text:
aln = lg.alignment("out/aligned_to_hg38.bam")
lg.check_step("call", {"aln": aln, "ref": hxb2})

DimensionError in step `call`:
  aln.reference = 2 contigs, 40 bp [fingerprint 6b927a061a81] (from SAM @SQ header: other.sam)
  ref.reference = 2 contigs, 40 bp [fingerprint aa185c059780] (from FASTA contigs: bare.fasta)
  Contig `1`: same name and length but different sequence (MD5 44e7acaf against a965a71a).
  These must match. Did you pass the wrong reference?

Note what caught this: the two references have the same contig names and the same lengths. Only the checksum separates them. Because neither carried a label, the message falls back to fingerprints so the two sides are distinguishable.

docs.title: chr1 against 1
docs.text:
ContigNamingError in step `call`:
  aln.contig_naming = chr-prefixed (UCSC style) (from SAM @SQ header: prefixed.sam)
  ref.contig_naming = bare (Ensembl/NCBI style) (from FASTA deflines: bare.fasta)
  The contigs are otherwise identical. Add a renaming step, or use one naming style throughout.

A distinct error, because it needs a distinct fix. The sequences are identical; only the names differ.

docs.title: Contigs in a different order
docs.text:
ContigOrderError in step `call`:
  aln.reference lists contigs in the order 2, 1 (from SAM @SQ header: reordered.sam)
  ref.reference lists contigs in the order 1, 2 (from FASTA contigs: bare.fasta)
  The contigs agree but their order differs. Tools that require a matching sequence
  dictionary order, such as GATK, will reject this.

docs.title: A shuffled sample set
docs.text:
DimensionError in step `merge`:
  one.sample_set = [sample_a, sample_b] (from VCF header sample columns: two_samples.vcf)
  two.sample_set = [sample_b, sample_a] (from VCF header sample columns: swapped.vcf)
  The same samples appear in both, in a different order.
  These must match, in order. Did the sample order change upstream?

docs.title: Something that must be declared
docs.text:
UndeclaredDimensionError in step `resistance`:
  aln.sample_set is unknown (no @RG lines with an SM tag in the header)
  v.sample_set = [sample_a] (from VCF header sample columns: calls.vcf)
  `resistance` needs sample_set to agree. Declare it where you load the data.

Take the advice:

aln = lg.alignment("out/sample.bam", samples=["sample_a"])

docs.title: Catching errors
docs.text:
The exceptions form a hierarchy, so you can be as specific as you need:

try:
    lg.check_step("call", {"aln": aln, "ref": hxb2})
except lg.ContigNamingError:
    ...                      # insert a renaming step
except lg.DimensionError:
    raise                    # anything else is a real problem

ContigNamingError, ContigOrderError and UndeclaredDimensionError all subclass DimensionError, which subclasses Exception.

docs.title: Getting every error at once
docs.text:
check_step raises the first disagreement, but all of them are found before anything is raised:

>>> try:
...     lg.check_step("call", bindings)
... except lg.DimensionError as error:
...     for each in error.errors:
...         print(each)

Or do not raise at all:

>>> for error in lg.dimension_errors("call", {"aln": aln, "ref": hxb2}):
...     print(error)

dimension_errors returns a list and never raises. For a whole pipeline rather than one step, use lg.Pipeline(...).errors(), which also knows what each step requires of the ones before it.

docs.title: Overriding what was inferred
docs.text:
Every loader takes keyword arguments for the dimensions a user can state:

# The filename is weak evidence for a sample name; say it outright.
reads = lg.reads("data/reads/x_1.fastq.gz", "data/reads/x_2.fastq.gz",
                 sample="patient_07", organism="HIV-1")

# Override the @RG SM tags.
aln = lg.alignment("out/sample.bam", samples=["patient_07"], organism="HIV-1")

A declared value wins over an inferred one, and the provenance says declared, so the error messages stay honest about where the value came from.

What you cannot override is reference identity. build= sets a display label only:

# This does not make the file hg38. If its contigs say otherwise, check() says so.
ref = lg.reference("refs/mystery.fa", build="hg38")

That is deliberate. A label that could override identity would be a way to silence the check, and the check is the product.

docs.title: Intervals: the format is the dimension
docs.text:
A BED or GFF carries its coordinate convention, and that convention is the whole reason the type exists:

>>> lg.intervals("data/regions.bed").dimension("coordinates").value
'0-based half-open'
>>> lg.intervals("data/genes.gff3").dimension("coordinates").value
'1-based closed'

It is taken from the filename, and never guessed. Pass format= when the name does not say:

>>> lg.intervals("data/regions.txt")
LoadError: cannot parse data/regions.txt: cannot tell whether this is a bed or
a gff from its name; pass the format explicitly
>>> regions = lg.intervals("data/regions.txt", format="bed")

Guessing would shift every interval by one base, which nothing downstream would notice — the same reason a FASTQ in the Phred+33/+64 overlap reports its encoding as unknown.

organism and build are declared, as for any other type. Contigs are not declarable at all: they come from the records, and there is no way to state them, which is why no step ever demands that an interval file know its reference.
