docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Python 3.11 or newer Rust a stable toolchain (rustup) A C compiler cc, for the bundled SQLite curl for fetching test data minimap2, samtools, bcftools only to run the HIV-1 reference demo

Rust is needed because installing builds the engine from source. There are no pre-built wheels yet.

The C compiler is needed because the cache bundles SQLite and compiles it, rather than linking whatever version the machine happens to have. That costs you a C toolchain at install time and buys an identical SQLite everywhere, which matters for an on-disk format the cache has to keep reading. If you are missing one, see below.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:Neoforge-Labs/ligase.git
cd ligase
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e ".[dev]"

The first build takes a minute or two while pyo3 compiles. Later builds are incremental.

Check it worked:

python -c "import ligase; print(ligase.__version__)"

0.1.0

The distribution and the import have different names

The PyPI distribution is ligase-bio but you import ligase. So it is pip install ligase-bio and import ligase. The distribution name ligase is already taken on PyPI by an unrelated project, and the import name is the one you actually live with, so that is the one that stayed short.

docs.title: Run the checks
docs.text:
The same gate CI runs, in the order it runs them:

cargo fmt --all --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace
ruff check .
ruff format --check .
mypy
pytest

All seven should pass on a clean checkout. If clippy complains about a missing doc comment on something you just added, that is deliberate — the workspace sets missing_docs to warn and CI runs clippy with -D warnings, so public items without documentation fail the build.

pytest passing is not the pipeline working

Nine tests need the demo's tools or its data: the five acceptance tests in tests/test_demo.py, and four in test_types.py and test_pipeline.py that want the real HXB2 or a BAM a real aligner wrote. They skip where either is missing, so a green pytest on a bare checkout says nothing about the pipeline. To insist instead:

LIGASE_DEMO_REQUIRED=1 pytest

Under that variable each of those skips becomes a failure naming what was missing. The demo job in CI sets it, which is what stops a green build from meaning "politely declined".

docs.title: Rebuilding after a Rust change
docs.text:
An editable install does not recompile on import. After editing anything under crates/, rebuild:

maturin develop

Or pip install -e . again, which is slower but equivalent. Forgetting this is the single most common confusion in a mixed Rust/Python project: your Python changes take effect immediately and your Rust changes do not.

docs.title: Test data
docs.text:
The reference pipeline runs on real HIV-1 data. It is downloaded rather than committed, into a gitignored data/:

scripts/fetch_test_data.sh

==> Reference: HXB2 (K03455.1)
  downloading from NCBI
  verified: 9719 bp, canonical SHA-256 matches

==> Reads: PRJNA1218827
  SRR32217714_1.fastq.gz verified
  ...
  4 runs ready in data/reads/PRJNA1218827

You get:

Path What data/refs/HXB2.fasta HIV-1 HXB2 reference, NCBI K03455.1, 9719 bp data/reads/PRJNA517147/ 4 paired runs, ~100 MB — published resistance results data/reads/PRJNA1218827/ 4 paired runs, ~30 MB — Sanger ground truth

Useful flags:

scripts/fetch_test_data.sh --list                     # show the manifest
scripts/fetch_test_data.sh --project PRJNA1218827     # just the small set
scripts/fetch_test_data.sh --reference-only           # just HXB2
scripts/fetch_test_data.sh --force                    # re-download

Set LIGASE_DATA_DIR to put the data somewhere else — useful if you keep large files on another volume.

docs.title: What the script guarantees
docs.text:
Every file is verified against a checksum pinned in the script, and the script exits non-zero if one does not match. Re-running is safe and cheap: files already on disk that verify are not downloaded again, so this doubles as an integrity check on data you fetched weeks ago.

Reads are pinned by ENA's own per-file MD5. The reference is pinned by the SHA-256 of its canonical sequence — sequence only, uppercased, line breaks removed — rather than of the raw file. This is decision D4 applied to an input: NCBI can reflow a FASTA or reword a defline without the biology changing, and a cosmetic change upstream must not break your build. A real change to the sequence still fails, loudly.

FASTQs come from ENA over HTTPS, so no SRA toolkit is required — only curl.

docs.title: The tools the demo runs
docs.text:
The reference pipeline shells out to three external tools. The rest of Ligase does not need them; the demo and the nine tests that drive it do.

Tool Version the demo is signed off on minimap2 2.31 samtools 1.24 bcftools 1.24 
brew install minimap2 samtools bcftools              # macOS

micromamba install -c conda-forge -c bioconda \
    minimap2=2.31 samtools=1.24 bcftools=1.24        # anywhere

Which versions you have matters more here than it usually would. A step's cache key includes its tools' versions, so upgrading minimap2 invalidates every alignment it produced — correctly, since a new aligner may genuinely align differently. That is also why CI pins all three from bioconda in .github/demo-tools.yml rather than taking whatever apt offers: an aligner that moved on its own would present as a Ligase regression, and the job is there to catch Ligase regressions.

docs.title: Build the docs
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[docs]"
mkdocs serve

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000. CI builds with mkdocs build --strict, so a broken internal link fails the build rather than shipping.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
No module named 'ligase' after a successful install. You are probably in a different interpreter than the one you installed into. Check with python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)".

Rust changes have no effect. Run maturin develop. See above.

error: linker 'cc' not found. No C toolchain. On Debian or Ubuntu, apt install build-essential; on macOS, xcode-select --install.

mkdocs build --strict fails on a link you just added. Internal links are relative to the file they live in, and must include the .md extension — ../decisions.md, not /decisions.

docs.title: Example notebooks
docs.text:
Four marimo notebooks, easiest first. They are ordinary Python files, so they run as notebooks or as scripts, and they are executed on every docs build — if the API drifts from what they claim, the build fails rather than the page misleading you.

Notebook What it shows 1 What a dataset knows Dimensions, and the provenance of each one 2 An error before compute A naming mismatch caught with nothing executed 3 A graph that has not run Per-sample fan-out, and every error in one pass 4 Resistance, and why the rules are hashed Vendored algorithms, and content hashing over version labels

docs.title: Running them
docs.text:
pip install ligase-bio marimo
marimo edit examples/notebooks/01_what_a_dataset_knows.py

Or without marimo at all, since a marimo notebook is importable Python:

python examples/notebooks/01_what_a_dataset_knows.py

The first three need no data and no aligner — they use the tiny fixtures committed with the test suite, so they work on a fresh clone. The fourth runs the real interpretation if the HIV-1 demo data is present, and explains itself if it is not:

scripts/fetch_test_data.sh --project PRJNA1218827

docs.title: Why they are not interactive on this page
docs.text:
marimo can export a notebook that runs in the browser, through Pyodide. Ligase cannot use that: it is a compiled Rust extension, and there is no emscripten wheel for it — the published wheels are manylinux, macOS and Windows. Building one would mean PyO3 and a bundled SQLite compiled for emscripten, which is not a realistic target.

So these are rendered from real runs and meant to be downloaded and run locally, where the engine actually works. The honest version of "interactive docs" for a native extension is a notebook you can run, not an iframe that cannot import the thing it documents.

docs.title: The full pipeline
docs.text: The notebooks are deliberately small. For the reference pipeline end to end — reads, alignment, variant calls, resistance — see examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py and running a pipeline.

docs.title: Reading what the engine noticed
docs.text:
A run can succeed and still have something to tell you about what it produced. That is a note: a statement about an output that its hash cannot carry.

There are two kinds, and this page covers both. One is something wrong with the file — a sample identifier that is a file name rather than a sample, which is the note that cost a reproducibility bundle its verification. The other is an assumption the step's own work rested on, which nothing in the file it wrote would show: a resistance reading made without coverage, or one whose codons did not all reach the depth it asked for.

The first has a fix. The second often does not, and is worth reading anyway, because it is the difference between a score and a floor.

For why the engine says either rather than refusing or repairing, see What a result rests on.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
$ ligase run
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525904)   4.5s
ran       `call` (sample SRR8525904)    513ms

noticed   `call` (sample SRR8525904): the sample identifier `/Users/kelyn/ligase/.ligase/store/62/7db9fa0cbac.bam` is an absolute path, not a sample
          Write the read group — `samtools addreplacerg -r ID:<sample> -r SM:<sample>` — so the calls below it name the sample.

8 steps: 8 ran.

Three things to read off that:

  • The line begins noticed, not failed. The step ran and its output is in the store. Nothing was lost and nothing has to be rerun before you can look at the result.
  • It names its node, the same way a check error does: you are told which step and which sample, not that something somewhere is wrong.
  • The instruction is said once, however many samples are affected.

docs.title: Why it happened
docs.text:
bcftools reads a VCF's sample name from the alignment's @RG SM field. minimap2 does not write a read group, so there is nothing to read — and bcftools falls back to naming the sample column after the input file's path, which in a Ligase run is a file inside the content-addressed store.

The same thing happens to a BAM whose read group names a file, and to any other tool that reaches for a filename when it cannot find an identifier.

docs.title: The fix
docs.text:
Write the read group where the alignment is made, so that every file below it carries the sample it is actually about:

@lg.step(tool=("minimap2", "samtools"))
def align(reads: Reads, ref: Reference, sample_id: str, threads: int = 4) -> Alignment:
    """Align one sample's reads against the reference."""
    return lg.sh(
        "minimap2 -t {threads} -ax sr {ref} {reads.r1} {reads.r2} "
        "| samtools addreplacerg -r ID:{sample_id} -r SM:{sample_id} -u -o - - "
        "| samtools sort -@ {threads} -o {out}"
    )

sample_id is an ordinary typed parameter, so pass the sample's own identifier when you build the pipeline:

samples = lg.samples("data/runs/*.fastq.gz", paired=True)

pipe = lg.Pipeline(
    [
        call(align(sample, hxb2, sample_id=run), hxb2)
        for run, sample in zip(samples.ids, samples, strict=True)
    ]
)

samples.ids is where the identifier comes from — the run accession lg.samples() read off the filename — so nothing here is invented, and the .map() shorthand is traded for a comprehension that can see both.

It will not split your cache

A parameter whose value is only the sample's own identifier is not a difference in how a step was run, so it does not give each sample its own sentence in the methods section and does not make the samples look like separate ways of running align.

Run it again and the note is gone:

$ ligase run
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525904)   4.5s
ran       `call` (sample SRR8525904)    498ms

8 steps: 8 ran.

The alignments changed — they carry a read group now — so everything below them reruns once. After that the pipeline is portable: the calls are named after run accessions, and their canonical hashes no longer depend on where your cache is.

docs.title: When a reading hedges
docs.text:
The other kind needs no fixing in the same sense: the step did what was asked, and is telling you what that rested on. The one to watch for is the alignment:

@lg.step(tool="hivdb")
def resistance(v: Variants, ref: Reference) -> ResistanceReport:
    return lg.hivdb.interpret(v, ref)          # no coverage

$ ligase run
ran       `resistance` (sample SRR8525904)   1.2s

noticed   `resistance` (sample SRR8525904): no alignment was supplied, so coverage is unknown, no codon can be phased, and every position the caller did not report is taken to be reference
          Pass the alignment — `coverage=aln` — so uncalled positions are reported as unread rather than as reference.

3 steps: 3 ran.

That one is a fix, and it is the advice: pass the alignment.

@lg.step(tool="hivdb")
def resistance(v: Variants, ref: Reference, aln: Alignment) -> ResistanceReport:
    return lg.hivdb.interpret(v, ref, coverage=aln)

What you get back instead is the truth about the coverage you actually have, which on a real amplicon run is usually not silence:

$ ligase run
ran       `resistance` (sample SRR8525904)   1.2s
ran       `resistance` (sample SRR8525908)   3.6s

noticed   `resistance` (sample SRR8525904): no codon of CA reached 100-fold coverage, so no drug scored against it could be assessed
noticed   `resistance` (sample SRR8525904): 220 of RT's 560 codons reached 100-fold coverage; the rest are reported as unread rather than as reference
noticed   `resistance` (sample SRR8525908): no codon of IN reached 100-fold coverage, so no drug scored against it could be assessed
          Sequence deeper, or lower the depth this reading asks for — `depth=` — so this gene's drugs can be assessed at all.
          Read a drug whose `unread` column is not empty as a floor, and sequence deeper to close it.

6 steps: 6 ran.

Read those as follows:

  • A gene no codon of which was read. Its drugs are in the report with every position they name listed as unread. That is no data, not a negative result — these samples are PR/RT amplicons, so capsid was never sequenced and lenacapavir cannot be assessed from them.
  • A gene partly read. Every drug whose rules mention an unread position has its score read as a floor: the mutations it looks for were not all looked at.
  • Codons no read spans. Read base by base, so they can name a mutation no single read carries, which errs towards reporting resistance rather than away from it (D31). Longer reads are the only real answer.

None of these changes a number in the report, and none of them is a failure. What they change is how far you should trust a susceptible call.

A lowered depth is not more coverage

depth=50 makes more codons count as read and makes these notes quieter. It does not make the reads exist. The honest use of it is deciding what depth a result should rest on, in the open, where the methods paragraph will say so.

docs.title: Reading it from Python
docs.text:
Every finished step carries its notes, so a script can act on them rather than grep the report:

report = pipe.run()

for step in report.steps:
    for note in step.notes:
        print(f"{step.step} ({step.sample}): {note}")

call (SRR8525904): the sample identifier `/Users/kelyn/…/7db9fa0cbac.bam` is an absolute path, not a sample
resistance (SRR8525904): 220 of RT's 560 codons reached 100-fold coverage; the rest are reported as unread rather than as reference

To fail a CI job on one, which is a reasonable thing to want of a pipeline that is supposed to be reproducible:

noticed = [step for step in report.steps if step.notes]
if noticed:
    raise SystemExit(f"{len(noticed)} outputs have something to say")

Or to refuse only the one assumption you will not accept, which for a clinical report is usually the coverage one:

blind = [
    step
    for step in report.steps
    for note in step.notes
    if "coverage is unknown" in note
]
if blind:
    raise SystemExit("a resistance report was interpreted without coverage")

docs.title: Where else it shows up
docs.text:
A note is stored with the result, not just printed once, so it is still there when nothing ran:

$ ligase run
cached    `call` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942

noticed   `call` (sample SRR8525904): the sample identifier `/Users/…/7db9fa0cbac.bam` is an absolute path, not a sample
          Write the read group — `samtools addreplacerg -r ID:<sample> -r SM:<sample>` — so the calls below it name the sample.

12 steps: 12 from cache.

A cache hit never reopens the file, so the note comes out of the cache beside the hash. A warning that appeared on the first run and vanished on the second would be worse than no warning at all.

It also reaches the three places a result is written up:

ligase methods says it after the paragraph and the references, so it is outside the prose you would paste into a manuscript:

$ ligase methods
`call` ran on 4 samples (SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942)
with bcftools 1.24, as `bcftools mpileup -a AD -f {ref} {aln} | ...`.

`call` ran on 4 samples (SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942),
where the sample identifier `/Users/kelyn/…/7db9fa0cbac.bam` is an absolute
path, not a sample — and the same for `/Users/kelyn/…/0c4e18baf21.bam`,
`/Users/kelyn/…/3a81d90ecc7.bam` and `/Users/kelyn/…/f20b7e4a115.bam`. A
sample set is a dimension, so the identifier is hashed exactly as the file
writes it. …

A bundle records every note in notes.tsv and gains a What was noticed section in its README.md. The table is always written, even when it is just a header line, so a reader never has to wonder whether an empty file means "nothing to report" or "an older bundle".

ligase methods --verify reports the first kind beside the verdicts, because a sample identifier that is a file is the second thing that explains a differs with no science behind it. A reading's hedges are not listed there: they are the same on every machine, so offering one as an explanation for a hash that moved would send you after the wrong thing.

$ ligase methods --verify bundle/
differs          `call` (SRR8525904)
    expected 9680fe10563f and got 4c1b77ae0d92

1 of 4 results name a file where a sample identifier belongs:
    `call` (SRR8525904): the sample identifier `/Users/…/7db9fa0cbac.bam` is an absolute path, not a sample
Such a hash depends on the file it was named after, so a `differs` here may be that and nothing else.
    Write the read group — `samtools addreplacerg -r ID:<sample> -r SM:<sample>` — so the calls below it name the sample.

4 results: 3 reproduced, 1 differs.

docs.title: What is not covered
docs.text:
• Inputs you supply yourself. Notes are about what a run produced. A VCF handed to the pipeline as a leaf input with path-shaped sample names is your file, described as you gave it, and nothing is said about it.
  • Every other way an identifier can be wrong. A sample column holding sample1 when it should hold SRR8525904 is a mistake no engine can see. What is detectable here is a file shape, and only that.
  • Anything about whether the calls are right. That is M6.
  • A shell step's assumptions. A body can say what its work rested on; a command cannot be asked. A step that shells out and wants to hedge has to say it in the file it writes.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: If you want to Read Know why the engine notices rather than refuses What a result rests on Know how a note is built, stored and said Notes Have a step of your own say what it rested on Notes Know what coverage buys a reading Interpreting resistance Write up a run, with or without notes Writing up a pipeline

docs.title: Writing up a pipeline
docs.text:
ligase methods says how your results were produced, and --bundle packages that up so someone else can check it.

This guide uses the HIV-1 demo. If you have not fetched its data yet, see installation; every command below also works on a pipeline of your own.

docs.title: The methods paragraph
docs.text:
$ ligase methods examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py
writing up 12 steps in examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py

Analyses were run with Ligase 0.1.0 on macos-aarch64.

`align` ran on 4 samples (SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942)
with minimap2 2.31-r1302 and samtools 1.24, as `minimap2 -t {threads} -ax sr
{ref} {reads.r1} {reads.r2} | samtools sort -@ {threads} -o {out}`, with
threads = 4, against the HXB2 reference (K03455.1, 9719 bp, MD5
c66838498aab02f786a6ec2f2d62cdc1).

`call` ran on 4 samples (SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942)
with bcftools 1.24, as `bcftools mpileup -a AD -f {ref} {aln} | bcftools
call -mv --ploidy 1 -Oz | bcftools view -i '(AD[0:1])/(AD[0:0]+AD[0:1]) >=
{min_freq}' -Oz -o {out}`, with min_freq = 0.01, against the HXB2 reference
(K03455.1, 9719 bp, MD5 c66838498aab02f786a6ec2f2d62cdc1).

`resistance` ran on 4 samples (SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920,
SRR8525942), by a function in the pipeline itself.

References

Danecek P, Bonfield JK, Liddle J, Marshall J, Ohan V, Pollard MO, Whitwham
    A, Keane T, McCarthy SA, Davies RM, Li H (2021) Twelve years of SAMtools
    and BCFtools. GigaScience 10(2):giab008. doi:10.1093/gigascience/giab008
Li H (2018) Minimap2: pairwise alignment for nucleotide sequences.
    Bioinformatics 34(18):3094-3100. doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/bty191

Four things are in there, and they are the four M5 is signed off on: the version every tool actually ran at, every parameter as it was hashed, the reference by accession and checksum, and the references to cite.

The wording is yours to fix; the facts are not yours to check

Every sentence follows a fixed form, and it will read like a machine wrote it, because one did. That is deliberate: a generator free to phrase things fluently would also be free to leave something out, and leaving something out is the one thing a methods section must not do. Rewrite the prose. Do not re-verify the versions.

The pipeline is run first, normally and through the cache, because a provenance record is filed under a step's key and computing keys is what a run does. A pipeline already computed costs a cache lookup per step:

$ time ligase methods examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py
...
1.127 total

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
methods = pipe.methods()
print(methods.text)

for step in methods.steps:
    print(step.step, step.nodes, step.tools, step.parameters)

for pinned in methods.references:
    print(pinned.accession, pinned.checksum)

methods.accounted_for is False when something could not be explained, and methods.gaps says which steps those were.

docs.title: Citing a tool the engine does not know
docs.text:
Ligase has checked references for the tools its reference pipeline uses — minimap2, samtools, bcftools. For anything else, say what to cite:

@lg.step(tool="fastp", cite="Chen S et al. (2018) fastp. Bioinformatics 34(17):i884.")
def trim(reads: Reads) -> Reads:
    return lg.sh("fastp -i {reads.r1} -I {reads.r2} --stdout | gzip > {out}")

Without it, the tool is reported as uncited rather than dropped from the reference list:

No reference is recorded for fastp. Add one with `@lg.step(cite=...)`, or
cite it by hand.

A citation never joins the cache key. It cannot change a result, so adding one to a step does not recompute a cohort.

docs.title: The reproducibility bundle
docs.text:
$ ligase methods examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py --bundle paper/bundle
...
wrote 13 files to paper/bundle

paper/bundle/
├── METHODS.md          the paragraph and the reference list
├── README.md           what this is, and how to check it
├── results.tsv         every output by content hash -- the claim
├── commands.tsv        the command that produced each one, as it ran
├── inputs.tsv          every input by content hash
├── notes.tsv           what canonicalising an output noticed; usually empty
├── references.tsv      every reference by accession and checksum
├── environment.tsv     the engine, the platform, every tool's full version
├── steps/              the source of every step
├── pipeline/           the pipeline file itself
└── MANIFEST            every file above, hashed, so damage is visible

commands.tsv holds what a cache hit can no longer prove:

align  SRR8525904  31f5306...  minimap2 -t '4' -ax sr '/…/HXB2.fasta' '/…/SRR8525904_1.fastq.gz' …

notes.tsv holds what the engine noticed about the outputs — a field that could not be dropped and was still wrong, or an assumption a step's work rested on. There is a header line even when there is nothing under it, so an empty file never has to be read as "an older bundle". A bundle with something in it gains a What was noticed section in its README.md.

The data is not in there. Sequencing runs are gigabytes and a bundle is meant to be readable, so inputs are named rather than carried — every one by content hash, every reference by accession and checksum. Fetch them by those identifiers; nothing else will pass the check.

docs.title: Checking a bundle
docs.text:
With the data in place:

$ ligase methods examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py --verify paper/bundle
...
identical        `align` (SRR8525904)
    the same key, the same result   43c4c32bbd53
identical        `call` (SRR8525904)
    the same key, the same result   79224f737eeb
...

12 results: 12 identical.

identical means nothing that feeds the computation moved. On someone else's machine the usual answer is the more interesting one:

reproduced       `align` (SRR8525904)
    the result is the same          43c4c32bbd53
    the key is not: something in the environment moved

A different key and the same result: their minimap2 is a different build, or their platform is, and the alignments came out the same anyway. That is the claim a bundle exists to let someone make.

When something really moved:

differs          `call` (SRR8525904)
    expected 79224f737eeb and got 4b1c90ea2277

1 of 12 inputs are not the ones this bundle was built from:
    changed    `reads` of `align`: data/reads/PRJNA517147/SRR8525904_1.fastq.gz
A changed input explains a changed output, so read these first.

The input lines come first for a reason: a differs with a changed input is a different experiment, not an irreproducible one.

checked = pipe.methods(verify="paper/bundle").verification
assert checked.reproduced, checked.text

for check in checked.differing:
    print(check.step, check.scope, check.expected, check.found)
for moved in checked.moved:
    print(moved.path, moved.presence)

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code When 0 Everything accounted for, and any bundle checked out. 1 A step could not be accounted for, or a result differs from the bundle. 2 The pipeline could not be read, or --verify was not pointed at a bundle.

docs.title: What this does not do
docs.text:
Fetch the data. Pinning by accession and checksum is as far as v0.1 goes (D8); a bundle tells you exactly which files it needs and checks the ones it finds.

Validate the results against published ones. That is M6, and a whole milestone, because agreeing with a paper is a scientific question rather than a hashing one.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• How was this produced? — why any of this exists, and what D22 cost.
  • Provenance architecture — the store, the paragraph and the bundle from the inside.
  • Semantic hashing and auditing — the other question about a result: does it repeat?

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Ligase ships twice from one tag: the engine as the ligase crate on crates.io, and the Python package as ligase-bio on PyPI.

Publishing is never automatic. .github/workflows/release.yml runs on a manual trigger whose default uploads nothing, and on a v* tag.

docs.title: Why wheels matter here
docs.text:
rusqlite is built with its bundled feature, so building from source compiles SQLite from C as well as the Rust engine. Someone installing from an sdist needs a Rust toolchain and a C compiler. For the people this is for — scientists, often in a notebook — that is a wall, so the release builds wheels and the sdist is only a fallback.

Because crates/ligase-py is built against abi3-py311, one wheel serves every Python from 3.11 upwards. The matrix is five builds, not twenty:

Platform Target Linux x86_64, aarch64 (manylinux) macOS aarch64, x86_64 Windows x64

A wheel that still needs a compiler would defeat the point, so the verify-wheel job installs the Linux wheel into a fresh virtualenv with cargo removed from PATH and fails if import ligase or ligase --help does not work. It fails loudly if cargo is still reachable, because then the test would prove nothing.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text: Two steps need account access and cannot be done from a workflow or by an assistant. Do them once.

docs.title: 1. PyPI Trusted Publishing
docs.text:
Trusted Publishing lets PyPI verify the workflow's OIDC identity, so no API token is ever stored in this repository. Create a pending publisher at https://pypi.org/manage/account/publishing/ with exactly these values:

Field Value PyPI project name ligase-bio Owner Neoforge-Labs Repository name ligase Workflow name release.yml Environment name pypi

Repeat it on https://test.pypi.org/manage/account/publishing/ with the environment testpypi if you want to rehearse against TestPyPI.

Then create the matching GitHub environments (Settings → Environments): pypi, testpypi, and crates-io. Adding required reviewers to pypi and crates-io is worth it — publishing cannot be undone.

docs.title: 2. A crates.io token
docs.text:
crates.io has no OIDC equivalent, so this one is a secret. Generate a token scoped to publish-new and publish-update at https://crates.io/settings/tokens, then add it as CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN in the crates-io environment — not as a repository-wide secret, so it is only readable by the job that publishes.

If you would rather not store a token at all, skip this and run cargo publish -p ligase from your own machine after cargo login. The workflow's rehearsal step still checks the crate packages correctly.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
1. Make sure main is green, including the demo job.
  2. Move the CHANGELOG.md entries under [Unreleased] into a new dated version section, and add its link at the bottom.
  3. Bump version in the workspace [workspace.package]. It is the single source of truth: the crate, the Python distribution and ligase.__version__ all inherit it, and a test asserts they agree.
  4. Rehearse. Run the workflow with dry-run: it builds every wheel, the sdist, verifies the wheel needs no toolchain, and runs cargo publish --dry-run, uploading nothing.
  5. Optionally run it with testpypi and install from there.
  6. Tag and push: git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "0.1.0" && git push origin v0.1.0. The tag publishes to both registries.

A manual run with publish does the same thing without a tag, for the case where a tag already exists.

docs.title: What cannot be undone
docs.text:
Both registries are append-only. crates.io has no delete, only cargo yank, which stops new dependents resolving to a version but leaves it downloadable. PyPI deletion is possible but the version number is burned forever: 0.1.0 can never be uploaded again, even deleted.

So the version number is spent the moment it uploads. Rehearse with dry-run first — that is what it is for.

docs.title: Interpreting resistance
docs.text:
A resistance step turns variant calls into a drug-by-drug report.

import ligase as lg
from ligase.types import Alignment, Reference, ResistanceReport, Variants


@lg.step(tool="hivdb")
def resistance(
    v: Variants,
    ref: Reference,
    aln: Alignment,
    mixture: float = 0.15,
) -> ResistanceReport:
    return lg.hivdb.interpret(v, ref, coverage=aln, mixture=mixture)

Run the reference demo and look at one:

ligase run examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py

gene  drug_class  drug  drug_name     score  level  interpretation                   mutations  unread
RT    NRTI        3TC   lamivudine    60     5      High-Level Resistance            M184V
RT    NRTI        AZT   zidovudine    -10    1      Susceptible                      M184V
IN    INSTI       DTG   dolutegravir  90     5      High-Level Resistance            T97A,E138T,G140S,Q148H
CA    CAI         LEN   lenacapavir   160    5      High-Level Resistance            M66I,Q67H,N74D,A105T

Negative scores are not a bug. M184V scores −10 for zidovudine, because it genuinely resensitises the virus to it, and Stanford's own reports carry the same number.

docs.title: The three arguments
docs.text:
interpret needs more than the calls, and neither addition is optional.

The reference is needed because a VCF holds only the positions that differ. Two of the three bases of a codon are usually not in it, so there is nothing to translate without the sequence those positions sit in. Passing it also puts it under check(), so interpreting one sample's calls against another organism's reference is refused before anything runs.

The alignment is needed for coverage and for phasing. Leave it out and two things happen:

  • every position the caller did not report is taken to be reference, which turns a sequencing dropout into a susceptible result; and
  • a codon with two ambiguous bases is read as every combination of them, including combinations no read carries.

The reading says so, in a note the run report prints and pipe.run() carries on the step:

noticed   `resistance` (sample SRR8525904): no alignment was supplied, so coverage is unknown, no codon can be phased, and every position the caller did not report is taken to be reference
          Pass the alignment — `coverage=aln` — so uncalled positions are reported as unread rather than as reference.

Not in the report file, because the report cannot show it: its unread column is empty when nothing is known to be unread, which is exactly what a fully covered sample looks like.

With the alignment the hedges that remain are about the coverage you actually have — a gene nobody sequenced deeply enough, a gene only partly read, a codon no read spans — and they arrive the same way. Reading what the engine noticed is about all of them.

The second one is why the reference demo passes coverage=aln even though the parameter is optional. With the alignment, reads spanning a codon are counted as the triplets they actually carry:

At a 2% threshold, RT codon 219 of Sample 3 Reads AAA — K 54% GAA — E 45% AGA — R 0.2% GGA — G 0.2%

Without the alignment all four are reported, because the caller credits G at 3204 in 43% of the reads and at 3205 in 2.4%, and the combinations of those are all four codons. With it the codon reads K219KE, which is what Stanford's own report for that sample says.

docs.title: Thresholds
docs.text:
Two separate numbers, because they answer different questions.

Parameter On Question min_freq the call step what fraction of reads must support an allele for it to be reported mixture the resistance step what fraction must support it for it to count as present

Keep min_freq low and set mixture to the threshold you are willing to act on. The published results Ligase is validated against use 2%, 5% and 15%, and the default is 0.15.

mixture is applied twice, to the two kinds of evidence: to an allele's share of the reads at its own position, as the caller counted them, and then to an amino acid's share of the reads that span its whole codon. The first says which alleles are there, the second which combinations of them are real.

The difference is not academic. On Sample 3 of PRJNA1218827:

mixture Result 0.15 K219KE — potential low-level resistance to two NRTIs 0.05 adds L100LI — high-level resistance to four NNRTIs

Same reads, same alignment, same algorithm. A 5% minority virus is the difference between "this regimen is fine" and "most of this class is already lost".

docs.title: Choosing an algorithm
docs.text:
lg.hivdb.ALGORITHMS      # ('HIVDB_10.2', 'HIVDB_9.8')
lg.hivdb.DEFAULT         # 'HIVDB_9.8'
lg.hivdb.fingerprint()   # what goes in the cache key

The default is the older of the two, deliberately: it is the version the published results in tests/test_validation.py were produced with, and a default that disagreed with the suite's own reference answers would make every validation run an argument about algorithm drift. Name algorithm="HIVDB_10.2" for the current science.

return lg.hivdb.interpret(v, ref, coverage=aln, algorithm="HIVDB_10.2")

Changing it reruns resistance and nothing above it, and the methods paragraph reports which one was used.

docs.title: What a report will not tell you
docs.text:
• A drug whose gene you did not sequence reads Not assessed, with no score. Lenacapavir is scored against capsid, which is in gag; a pol pipeline gets nothing for it, and saying "Susceptible" would be inventing a negative result.
  • A score resting on positions you did not cover is a floor. The unread column names them. The score is still the best lower bound available — a rule naming one of those positions might have matched.
  • Comments. Stanford's reports carry explanatory prose for each mutation; Ligase reports levels, scores and mutations. The comment text is in the vendored XML and is the obvious thing to add if a report ever wants it.

docs.title: Adding a newer algorithm
docs.text: See crates/ligase-core/rulesets/README.md. In short: drop the XML in, add a row to PROVENANCE.tsv with its SHA-256, run scripts/vendor_hivdb_algorithm.py --write, and run the tests.

docs.title: Running a pipeline
docs.text: Everything here runs today. Building a pipeline gets you as far as pipe.check(); this goes the rest of the way.

docs.title: Say how a step produces its output
docs.text:
A step's body is never asked to compute anything. It is called once, before the run starts, and what it returns says how the output is produced:

import ligase as lg
from ligase.types import Alignment, Reads, Reference, Variants


@lg.step(tool=("minimap2", "samtools"))
def align(reads: Reads, ref: Reference) -> Alignment:
    return lg.sh(
        "minimap2 -ax sr {ref} {reads.r1} {reads.r2} | samtools sort -o {out}"
    )

lg.sh builds a command; it does not run one, and it does not format the string. The engine fills the placeholders in once it knows where everything is:

Placeholder What it becomes {ref} the file bound to the parameter ref {reads.r1}, {reads.r2} the mates of a paired input {min_freq} a plain parameter's value {out} the file this step must write

Two rules are worth knowing before you write a long command.

{out} is the only output. A step that writes anywhere else has produced nothing, as far as the engine is concerned, and is reported as having finished without writing its output.

Every substituted value is one shell word. A path with a space in it stays one path. For a literal brace — an awk program, say — double it:

return lg.sh("awk '{{print $1, $4}}' {regions} > {out}")

That is Snakemake's convention, and it exists because {print $1} and {refrence} are otherwise indistinguishable: one of them is a typo you want to be told about.

docs.title: Name the tools a step calls
docs.text:
tool= is how a tool's version reaches the cache key:

@lg.step(tool="bcftools")                       # one tool
@lg.step(tool=("minimap2", "samtools"))         # a pipe of two

Each one's --version is hashed, so upgrading bcftools reruns the calling steps and nothing else. A tool that is not installed fails the step before it runs, naming the tool — a typo in tool="minimap" is a problem you want at second zero, not at hour six.

docs.title: Steps whose work is Python
docs.text:
Not everything shells out. lg.write hands the engine a function to call with the path to write to:

@lg.step
def resistance(v: Variants) -> ResistanceReport:
    return lg.write(lambda out: interpret(v.file, out))

v.file works inside the function because by the time it is called, the steps above it have run. Reading it earlier raises, and says so. It is typed as a path rather than an optional one for the same reason: a body reached through lg.write is a body whose inputs exist.

(v.path, which every dataset also has, is the honest answer to "where did this come from, if anywhere?" and so can be None. Use .file when you are about to open it.)

These steps take the GIL, so they do not run in parallel with each other — the right trade for an interpretation step, the wrong one for anything doing real work. Prefer lg.sh.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
pipe = lg.Pipeline(samples.map(lambda s: resistance(call(align(s, hxb2), hxb2))))

report = pipe.run()

Or from the command line:

$ ligase run pipeline.py
running 12 steps in pipeline.py

ran       `align` (sample SRR8525904)        4.5s
ran       `call` (sample SRR8525904)         513ms
ran       `resistance` (sample SRR8525904)   3ms
...

12 steps: 12 ran.

The pipeline is checked first, every time. A pipeline that does not type-check does not run at all:

$ ligase run pipeline.py
running 12 steps in pipeline.py

DimensionError in step `call` (sample SRR8525904):
  aln.reference = HXB2 (from step `align`)
  ref.reference = hg38 (from FASTA contigs: data/refs/hg38.fasta)
  These must match. Did you pass the wrong reference?

4 errors in 4 steps.
Option What it does -j N, --jobs N how many steps may run at once (default: one per core) --force run every step, cache or no cache --cache DIR where to keep the cache (default: ./.ligase)

ligase run exits 0 when everything worked, 1 when a step failed or the pipeline has errors, and 2 when the pipeline could not be read at all.

To ask whether a step repeats itself rather than whether it needs rerunning, see ligase audit.

docs.title: Read the report
docs.text:
report = pipe.run()

report.summary            # '12 steps: 3 ran, 9 from cache.'
len(report.ran)           # 3
report.outputs("call")    # one path per sample, in graph order

for step in report.steps:
    print(step.step, step.sample, step.outcome, step.duration_ms)

An outcome is one of three things:

  • ran — it ran.
  • cached — its key was already known, and nothing above it ran.
  • skipped — its key was already known although something above it reran, because that rerun produced the same output as before. This is early cutoff.

report.hashed and report.prefiltered say how many input files had to be read against how many were recognised from their size and modification time.

docs.title: When a step fails
docs.text:
pipe.run() raises, and the exception carries the whole run — including everything that did work, which for a cohort is usually most of it:

try:
    report = pipe.run()
except lg.RunError as error:
    print(error.report.text)
    for failure in error.report.failures:
        print(failure.step, failure.sample, failure.message)

One sample failing does not take the others down with it: independent branches keep going, and the steps below a failure are simply not run. A failure is reported once, against the node that caused it, in the tool's own words:

`align` (sample SRR8525942) failed:
  the command failed with exit status 1
  [E::sam_parse1] missing SAM header

11 steps: 9 ran, 1 from cache, 1 failed.

A failed step leaves nothing in the cache, so fixing the cause and running again retries exactly that step.

docs.title: Where the outputs are
docs.text:
In the store, named after the hash of their contents:

>>> report.outputs("resistance")
['/work/.ligase/store/3c/73431de6...eeaa85.tsv']

Reach them by asking the report, or through the handle the step returned:

aligned = align(sample, hxb2)
pipe = lg.Pipeline(call(aligned, hxb2))
pipe.run()

lg.handle(aligned).file    # where that alignment landed

The store is derived data. Deleting .ligase/ costs you a rerun and nothing else.

docs.title: Try it on the real thing
docs.text:
The repository ships the reference demo — HIV-1 reads, HXB2, real tools:

$ scripts/fetch_test_data.sh --project PRJNA517147
$ ligase run examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py

Then run it a second time, change min_freq in the file and run it again, and watch which steps come back.

docs.title: Semantic hashing and ligase audit
docs.text:
Semantic hashing needs nothing from you: it is how every step's inputs are hashed. This page is about seeing it work, and about the one command that asks a question it cannot answer on its own.

Everything below uses the reference demo. Fetch its data first if you have not:

scripts/fetch_test_data.sh --project PRJNA517147

docs.title: Watching a rerun stop
docs.text:
The demo's aligner takes a thread count:

@lg.step(tool=("minimap2", "samtools"))
def align(reads: Reads, ref: Reference, threads: int = 4) -> Alignment:
    return lg.sh(
        "minimap2 -t {threads} -ax sr {ref} {reads.r1} {reads.r2} "
        "| samtools sort -@ {threads} -o {out}"
    )

Run the demo, then run it again with more threads:

ligase run examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py

import importlib.util

spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(
    "demo", "examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py"
)
demo = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(demo)

report = demo.pipeline(threads=8).run()
print(report.text)

ran       `align` (sample SRR8525904)   3.3s
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525908)   6.9s
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525920)   3.7s
ran       `align` (sample SRR8525942)   6.0s
skipped   `call` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942
skipped   `resistance` for SRR8525904, SRR8525908, SRR8525920, SRR8525942

12 steps: 4 ran, 8 skipped.

align reran — threads is one of its parameters — and produced BAMs whose bytes differ from the first run's, because minimap2 writes -t 8 and the output path into its @PG line. The alignments did not change, so the variant calling and the reports below were not redone.

Every step reports both hashes, so you can see that for yourself:

for step in report.steps:
    print(f"{step.outcome:8} {step.step:12} {step.hash[:12]}  {step.canonical[:12]}")
  • hash is the output's bytes, which is also its name in the store.
  • canonical is what the output means. This is what the steps below were keyed on.

Two runs that agree on canonical skip everything downstream, however far their hash diverged.

docs.title: Auditing a step
docs.text:
ligase audit runs a step twice and tells you whether it agrees with itself. Use it when you are about to publish, when a collaborator cannot reproduce a number, or when a tool is new to you and you want to know what it does with a seed.

ligase audit align examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py --sample SRR8525904

auditing `align` for SRR8525904 in examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py

reproducible     `align` (sample SRR8525904)
    the bytes differ            36696dacb83d / a96bfeff4e26
    what they mean does not     43c4c32bbd53

1 step: 1 reproducible.

Three verdicts, and the middle one is the point:

Verdict What it means What to do deterministic The two runs wrote the same bytes. Nothing. reproducible The bytes differ; the result does not. Nothing. This is every tool that signs its own work. not reproducible The two runs disagree about the result. Find the unseeded randomness.

A tool that stamps the time of day into its output is reproducible, not broken — and an audit that tested bytes alone would report the entire reference pipeline as irreproducible, which is how a check gets ignored.

ligase audit resistance examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py --sample SRR8525904

deterministic    `resistance` (sample SRR8525904)
    the same bytes both times   75724d8c3179

1 step: 1 deterministic.

docs.title: Under fan-out
docs.text:
One written step is one step per sample, so ligase audit align audits every one of them and names each:

ligase audit align examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py

That is two runs of the aligner per sample, taken in turn — timings from runs fighting each other for cores would say more about the machine than about the step. --sample SRR8525904 narrows it to one.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
report = pipe.audit("align")

if not report.reproducible:
    for step in report.unreproducible:
        print(f"{step.step} for {step.sample} does not repeat")
        print(f"  {step.first_canonical} then {step.second_canonical}")

report.verdict is the worst verdict any node got, because one irreproducible sample in a cohort is an irreproducible step.

docs.title: What an audit does and does not touch
docs.text:
The pipeline is run first, normally and through the cache, so that the step being audited has its inputs — that part is an ordinary run and is recorded like one. The two audit runs then write into scratch files that are deleted, and nothing from them is recorded. An audit observes; it does not put a result from a step known to wobble into your cache.

A step that fails is reported as a failure rather than given a verdict, and the exit code is 1 for a finding (a step that does not repeat, or one that failed) and 2 for a mistake in the command, such as a step name nothing is called:

$ ligase audit allign examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py
ligase: no step named `allign` in examples/hiv-resistance/pipeline.py; it has `align`, `call`, `resistance`

docs.title: Making your own step reproducible
docs.text:
If an audit says not reproducible, the cause is almost always a number nobody wrote down.

Seed everything, as a parameter. A seed is an ordinary typed parameter, so it is hashed like any other and the engine will rerun the step when you change it:

@lg.step(tool="some-sampler")
def subsample(reads: Reads, fraction: float = 0.1, seed: int = 20260101) -> Reads:
    return lg.sh("some-sampler --seed {seed} --fraction {fraction} {reads.r1} -o {out}")

A step that draws on a seed it did not declare is not reproducible, and no cache can make it so.

Check the tool's own flags. Many tools are deterministic only when told to be, or only at a fixed batch size.

Remember what is already handled. You do not need to strip timestamps, sort a BAM for comparability, or normalise line wrapping — a format's volatile fields are already known, and samtools view -b of a SAM hashes the same as the SAM (D9).

docs.title: Seeing what it cost
docs.text:
report = pipe.run()
print(report.hashed, report.prefiltered, report.canonicalised)
  • hashed — files read and hashed.
  • prefiltered — files whose hash was already known from their size and mtime.
  • canonicalised — files parsed to find out what they mean.

On a second run all three of these are what you would hope:

again = pipe.run()
assert again.hashed == 0
assert again.canonicalised == 0

What a file means is remembered against the hash of its bytes, so it is parsed once and then never again — not on the next run, and not when a different step produces the same bytes.

docs.title: When a cache goes cold on its own
docs.text: A change to the canonicalisation rules retires every canonical hash made under the old ones, and the step entries built from them. You will see a run that recomputes everything after upgrading Ligase. Nothing is lost: all of it is derived, and recomputing is merely slow (D19).
